# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3

A simple to use, efficient, and full featured library for parsing command line arguments and subcommands when writing console, or terminal applications.

`clap` is used to parse *and validate* the string of command line arguments provided by the user at runtime. You provide the list of valid possibilities, and `clap` handles the rest. This means you focus on your *applications* functionality, and less on the parsing and validating of arguments.

`clap` also provides the traditional version and help switches (or flags) 'for free' meaning automatically with no configuration. It does this by checking list of valid possibilities you supplied and adding only the ones you haven't already defined. If you are using subcommands, `clap` will also auto-generate a `help` subcommand for you in addition to the traditional flags.

Once `clap` parses the user provided string of arguments, it returns the matches along with any applicable values. If the user made an error or typo, `clap` informs them of the mistake and exits gracefully (or returns a `Result` type and allows you to perform any clean up prior to exit). Because of this, you can make reasonable assumptions in your code about the validity of the arguments.

For a full FAQ and more in depth details, see [the wiki page](https://github.com/kbknapp/clap-rs/wiki/FAQ)

First, let me say that these comparisons are highly subjective, and not meant in a critical or harsh manner. All the argument parsing libraries out there (to include `clap`) have their own strengths and weaknesses. Sometimes it just comes down to personal taste when all other factors are equal. When in doubt, try them all and pick one that you enjoy :) There's plenty of room in the Rust community for multiple implementations!

`getopts` is a very basic, fairly minimalist argument parsing library. This isn't a bad thing, sometimes you don't need tons of features, you just want to parse some simple arguments, and have some help text generated for you based on valid arguments you specify. The downside to this approach is that you must manually implement most of the common features (such as checking to display help messages, usage strings, etc.). If you want a highly custom argument parser, and don't mind writing the majority of the functionality yourself, `getopts` is an excellent base.

`getopts` also doesn't allocate much, or at all. This gives it a very small performance boost. Although, as you start implementing additional features, that boost quickly disappears.

Personally, I find many, many uses of `getopts` are manually implementing features that `clap` provides by default. Using `clap` simplifies your codebase allowing you to focus on your application, and not argument parsing.

I first want to say I'm a big a fan of BurntSushi's work, the creator of `Docopt.rs`. I aspire to produce the quality of libraries that this man does! When it comes to comparing these two libraries they are very different. `docopt` tasks you with writing a help message, and then it parsers that message for you to determine all valid arguments and their use. Some people LOVE this approach, others do not. If you're willing to write a detailed help message, it's nice that you can stick that in your program and have `docopt` do the rest. On the downside, it's far less flexible.

`docopt` is also excellent at translating arguments into Rust types automatically. There is even a syntax extension which will do all this for you, if you're willing to use a nightly compiler (use of a stable compiler requires you to somewhat manually translate from arguments to Rust types). To use BurntSushi's words, `docopt` is also a sort of black box. You get what you get, and it's hard to tweak implementation or customize the experience for your use case.

Because `docopt` is doing a ton of work to parse your help messages and determine what you were trying to communicate as valid arguments, it's also one of the more heavy weight parsers performance-wise. For most applications this isn't a concern and this isn't to say `docopt` is slow, in fact from it. This is just something to keep in mind while comparing.

`clap` is as fast, and as lightweight as possible while still giving all the features you'd expect from a modern argument parser. In fact, for the amount and type of features `clap` offers it remains about as fast as `getopts`. If you use `clap` when just need some simple arguments parsed, you'll find its a walk in the park. `clap` also makes it possible to represent extremely complex, and advanced requirements, without too much thought. `clap` aims to be intuitive, easy to use, and fully capable for wide variety use cases and needs.

The following examples show a quick example of some of the very basic functionality of `clap`. For more advanced usage, such as requirements, conflicts, groups, multiple values and occurrences see the [documentation](http://kbknapp.github.io/clap-rs/clap/index.html), [examples/](https://docs.rs/examples) directory of this repository or the [video tutorials](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLza5oFLQGTl0Bc_EU_pBNcX-rhVqDTRxv) (which are quite outdated by now).

**NOTE:** All these examples are functionally the same, but show three different styles in which to use `clap`

The following example is show a method that allows more advanced configuration options (not shown in this small example), or even dynamically generating arguments when desired. The downside is it's more verbose.

// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01b_quick_example.rs) // // This example demonstrates clap's full 'builder pattern' style of creating arguments which is // more verbose, but allows easier editing, and at times more advanced options, or the possibility // to generate arguments dynamically. extern crate clap; use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand}; fn main() { let matches = App::new("My Super Program") .version("1.0") .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>") .about("Does awesome things") .arg(Arg::with_name("config") .short("c") .long("config") .value_name("FILE") .help("Sets a custom config file") .takes_value(true)) .arg(Arg::with_name("INPUT") .help("Sets the input file to use") .required(true) .index(1)) .arg(Arg::with_name("v") .short("v") .multiple(true) .help("Sets the level of verbosity")) .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test") .about("controls testing features") .version("1.3") .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>") .arg(Arg::with_name("debug") .short("d") .help("print debug information verbosely"))) .get_matches(); // Gets a value for config if supplied by user, or defaults to "default.conf" let config = matches.value_of("config").unwrap_or("default.conf"); println!("Value for config: {}", config); // Calling .unwrap() is safe here because "INPUT" is required (if "INPUT" wasn't // required we could have used an 'if let' to conditionally get the value) println!("Using input file: {}", matches.value_of("INPUT").unwrap()); // Vary the output based on how many times the user used the "verbose" flag // (i.e. 'myprog -v -v -v' or 'myprog -vvv' vs 'myprog -v' match matches.occurrences_of("v") { 0 => println!("No verbose info"), 1 => println!("Some verbose info"), 2 => println!("Tons of verbose info"), 3 | _ => println!("Don't be crazy"), } // You can handle information about subcommands by requesting their matches by name // (as below), requesting just the name used, or both at the same time if let Some(matches) = matches.subcommand_matches("test") { if matches.is_present("debug") { println!("Printing debug info..."); } else { println!("Printing normally..."); } } // more program logic goes here... }

The following example is functionally the same as the one above, but shows a far less verbose method but sacrifices some of the advanced configuration options (not shown in this small example).

// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01a_quick_example.rs) // // This example demonstrates clap's "usage strings" method of creating arguments which is less // less verbose extern crate clap; use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand}; fn main() { let matches = App::new("myapp") .version("1.0") .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>") .about("Does awesome things") .args_from_usage( "-c, --config=[FILE] 'Sets a custom config file' <INPUT> 'Sets the input file to use' -v... 'Sets the level of verbosity'") .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test") .about("controls testing features") .version("1.3") .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>") .arg_from_usage("-d, --debug 'Print debug information'")) .get_matches(); // Same as previous example... }

The following combines the previous two examples by using the less verbose `from_usage` methods and the performance of the Builder Pattern.

// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01c_quick_example.rs) // Must be compiled with `--features unstable` // // This example demonstrates clap's "usage strings" method of creating arguments which is less // less verbose #[macro_use] extern crate clap; fn main() { let matches = clap_app!(myapp => (version: "1.0") (author: "Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>") (about: "Does awesome things") (@arg config: -c --config +takes_value "Sets a custom config file") (@arg INPUT: +required "Sets the input file to use") (@arg verbose: -v ... "Sets the level of verbosity") (@subcommand test => (about: "controls testing features") (version: "1.3") (author: "Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>") (@arg verbose: -d --debug "Print debug information") ) ).get_matches(); // Same as previous examples... }

This final method shows how you can use a YAML file to build your CLI and keep your Rust source tidy or support multiple localized translations by having different YAML files for each localization. First, create the `cli.yml` file to hold your CLI options, but it could be called anything we like (we'll use the same both examples above to keep it functionally equivalent):

```
name: myapp
version: 1.0
author: Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>
about: Does awesome things
args:
    - config:
        short: c
        long: config
        value_name: FILE
        help: Sets a custom config file
        takes_value: true
    - INPUT:
        help: Sets the input file to use
        required: true
        index: 1
    - verbose:
        short: v
        multiple: true
        help: Sets the level of verbosity
subcommands:
    - test:
        about: controls testing features
        version: 1.3
        author: Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>
        args:
            - debug:
                short: d
                help: print debug information
```
Now we create our `main.rs` file just like we would have with the previous two examples:

// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/17_yaml.rs) // // This example demonstrates clap's building from YAML style of creating arguments which is far // more clean, but takes a very small performance hit compared to the other two methods. #[macro_use] extern crate clap; use clap::App; fn main() { // The YAML file is found relative to the current file, similar to how modules are found let yaml = load_yaml!("cli.yml"); let matches = App::from_yaml(yaml).get_matches(); // Same as previous examples... }

**NOTE**: The YAML and macro builder options require adding a special `features` flag when compiling `clap` because they are not compiled by default. Simply change your `clap = "2"` to `clap = {version = "2", features = ["yaml"]}` for YAML, or `features = ["unstable"]` for the macro builder, in your `Cargo.toml`.

If you were to compile any of the above programs and run them with the flag `--help` or `-h` (or `help` subcommand, since we defined `test` as a subcommand) the following would be output

$ myprog --help My Super Program 1.0 Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com> Does awesome things USAGE: MyApp [FLAGS] [OPTIONS] <INPUT> [SUBCOMMAND] FLAGS: -h, --help Prints this message -v Sets the level of verbosity -V, --version Prints version information OPTIONS: -c, --config <FILE> Sets a custom config file ARGS: INPUT The input file to use SUBCOMMANDS: help Prints this message test Controls testing features

**NOTE:** You could also run `myapp test --help` to see similar output and options for the `test` subcommand.

To try out the pre-built example, use the following steps:

- Clone the repository `$ git clone https://github.com/kbknapp/clap-rs && cd clap-rs/clap-tests`
- Compile the example `$ cargo build --release`
- Run the help info `$ ./target/release/claptests --help`
- Play with the arguments!

To test out `clap`'s default auto-generated help/version follow these steps:
* Create a new cargo project `$ cargo new fake --bin && cd fake`
* Add `clap` to your `Cargo.toml`
*
`toml [dependencies] clap = "2"`

- Add the following to your `src/main.rs`

extern crate clap; use clap::App; fn main() { App::new("fake").version("v1.0-beta").get_matches(); }

- Build your program `$ cargo build --release`
- Run with help or version `$ ./target/release/fake --help`or`$ ./target/release/fake --version`

For full usage, add `clap` as a dependency in your `Cargo.toml` file to use from crates.io:

```
 [dependencies]
 clap = "2"
```
Or track the latest on the master branch at github:

```
[dependencies.clap]
git = "https://github.com/kbknapp/clap-rs.git"
```
Add `extern crate clap;` to your crate root.

Define a list of valid arguments for your program (see the [documentation](https://kbknapp.github.io/clap-rs/index.html) or [examples/](https://docs.rs/examples) directory of this repo)

Then run `cargo build` or `cargo update && cargo build` for your project.

If you'd like to keep your dependency list to **only** `clap`, you can disable any features that require an additional dependency. To do this, add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.clap]
version = "2"
default-features = false
```
You can also selectively enable only the features you'd like to include, by adding:

```
[dependencies.clap]
version = "2"
default-features = false
# Cherry-pick the features you'd like to use
features = [ "suggestions", "color" ]
```
The following is a list of optional `clap` features:

- **"suggestions"**: Turns on the- `Did you mean '--myoption'?`feature for when users make typos.
- **"color"**: Turns on colored error messages. This feature only works on non-Windows OSs.
- **"lints"**: This is- **not**included by default and should only be used while developing to run basic lints against changes. This can only be used on Rust nightly.
- **"debug"**: This is- **not**included by default and should only be used while developing to display debugging information.
- **"yaml"**: This is- **not**included by default. Enables building CLIs from YAML documents.
- **"unstable"**: This is- **not**included by default. Enables unstable features, unstable refers to whether or not they may change, not performance stability.

You can find complete documentation on the [github-pages site](http://kbknapp.github.io/clap-rs/clap/index.html) for this project.

You can also find usage examples in the [examples/](https://docs.rs/examples) directory of this repo.

There's also the video tutorial series [Argument Parsing with Rust](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLza5oFLQGTl0Bc_EU_pBNcX-rhVqDTRxv) that I've been working on.

*Note*: Two new videos have just been added ([08 From Usage](https://youtu.be/xc6VdedFrG0), and [09 Typed Values](https://youtu.be/mZn3C1DnD90)), if you're already familiar with `clap` but want to know more about these two details you can check out those videos without watching the previous few.

*Note*: Apologies for the resolution of the first video, it will be updated to a better resolution soon. The other videos have a proper resolution.

If contributing, you can run the tests as follows (assuming you're in the `clap-rs` directory)

$ cargo test && make -C clap-tests test $ cargo test --features yaml $ cargo build --features lints

`clap` is licensed under the MIT license. Please read the [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT) file in this repository for more information.

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap/*

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`
- `snapbox`
- `assert_cmd`- `assert_fs`

Documentation:

# rustdoc_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/

## Expand description

Rustdoc’s JSON output interface

These types are the public API exposed through the `--output-format json` flag. The [ Crate](https://docs.rs/struct.Crate.html)
struct is the root of the JSON blob and all other items are contained within.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

[§](https://docs.rs#rustc-hash)`rustc-hash`

We expose a `rustc-hash` feature, disabled by default. This feature switches the
[ std::collections::HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html) for [

`rustc_hash::FxHashMap`] to improve the performance of said
`HashMap` in specific situations.`cargo-semver-checks` for example, saw a [-3% improvement](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/266220-t-rustdoc/topic/rustc-hash.20and.20performance.20of.20rustdoc-types/near/474855731) when benchmarking using the
`aws_sdk_ec2` JSON output (~500MB of JSON). As always, we recommend measuring the impact before
turning this feature on, as [ FxHashMap](https://crates.io/crates/rustc-hash) only concerns itself with hash speed, and may
increase the number of collisions.

[§](https://docs.rs#rkyv_0_8)`rkyv_0_8`

We expose a `rkyv_0_8` feature, disabled by default. When enabled, it derives `rkyv`’s
[ Archive](https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.15/rkyv/trait.Archive.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.15/rkyv/trait.Serialize.html)

`Serialize`[traits for all types in this crate. Furthermore, it exposes the corresponding](https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.15/rkyv/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize``Archived*` types (e.g. `ArchivedId` for [).](https://docs.rs/struct.Id.html)

`Id``rkyv` lets you works with JSON output without paying the deserialization cost *upfront*,
thanks to [zero-copy deserialization](https://rkyv.org/zero-copy-deserialization.html).
You can perform various types of analyses on the `Archived*` version of the relevant types,
incurring the full deserialization cost only for the subset of items you actually need.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocItemConstraint.html)- Item - Constraint
- Describes a bound applied to an associated type/constant.
- [Attribute](https://docs.rs/struct.AttributeRepr.html)- Repr
- The contents of a `#[repr(...)]`attribute.
- [Constant](https://docs.rs/struct.Constant.html)
- A constant.
- [Crate](https://docs.rs/struct.Crate.html)
- The root of the emitted JSON blob.
- [Deprecation](https://docs.rs/struct.Deprecation.html)
- Information about the deprecation of an `Item`
- [Discriminant](https://docs.rs/struct.Discriminant.html)
- The value that distinguishes a variant in an `Enum`
- [DynTrait](https://docs.rs/struct.DynTrait.html)
- Dynamic trait object type (`dyn Trait`).
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/struct.Enum.html)
- An `enum`.
- [External](https://docs.rs/struct.ExternalCrate.html)- Crate
- Metadata of a crate, either the same crate on which `rustdoc`was invoked, or its dependency.
- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.Function.html)
- A function declaration (including methods and other associated functions).
- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionHeader.html)- Header
- A set of fundamental properties of a function.
- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionPointer.html)- Pointer
- A type that is a function pointer.
- [Function](https://docs.rs/struct.FunctionSignature.html)- Signature
- The signature of a function.
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/struct.GenericParamDef.html)- Param - Def
- One generic parameter accepted by an item.
- [Generics](https://docs.rs/struct.Generics.html)
- Generic parameters accepted by an item and `where`clauses imposed on it and the parameters.
- [Id](https://docs.rs/struct.Id.html)
- An opaque identifier for an item.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/struct.Impl.html)
- An `impl`block.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.Item.html)
- Anything that can hold documentation - modules, structs, enums, functions, traits, etc.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemSummary.html)- Summary
- Information about an external (not defined in the local crate) `Item`
- [Module](https://docs.rs/struct.Module.html)
- A module declaration, e.g. `mod foo;`or`mod foo {}`.
- [Path](https://docs.rs/struct.Path.html)
- A type that has a simple path to it. This is the kind of type of structs, unions, enums, etc.
- [Poly](https://docs.rs/struct.PolyTrait.html)- Trait
- A trait and potential HRTBs
- [Primitive](https://docs.rs/struct.Primitive.html)
- A primitive type declaration. Declarations of this kind can only come from the core library.

# camel_xj - Rust

## Expand description

XML↔JSON conversion component powered by the xml-bridge.

Endpoint URI format:
`xj:<stylesheet>?direction=xml2json|json2xml[&transformDirection=XML2JSON|JSON2XML][&resourceUri=<uri>]`

Example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let xml_to_json = "xj:classpath:identity?direction=xml2json";
let json_to_xml = "xj:classpath:identity?direction=json2xml";
let with_options = "xj:file:///tmp/transform.xslt?direction=xml2json&transformDirection=XML2JSON&resourceUri=classpath:extra.xslt";
```

# gts_validator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gts-validator/0.11.0/gts_validator/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#gts-validator)gts-validator

GTS identifier validator for documentation and configuration files.

This crate provides a clean separation between the **core validation engine**
(input-agnostic) and **input strategies** (starting with filesystem scanning).

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use std::path::PathBuf;
use gts_validator::{validate_fs, FsSourceConfig, ValidationConfig, VendorPolicy};
let mut fs_config = FsSourceConfig::default();
fs_config.paths = vec![PathBuf::from("docs"), PathBuf::from("modules")];
fs_config.exclude = vec!["target/*".to_owned()];
let mut validation_config = ValidationConfig::default();
validation_config.vendor_policy = VendorPolicy::MustMatch("x".to_owned());
let report = validate_fs(&fs_config, &validation_config).unwrap();
println!("Files scanned: {}", report.scanned_files);
println!("Validation errors: {}", report.errors_count());
println!("Scan errors: {}", report.scan_errors.len());
println!("OK: {}", report.ok);
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [output](https://docs.rs/output/index.html)
- Shared output formatting for validation reports.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FsSource](https://docs.rs/struct.FsSourceConfig.html)- Config
- Filesystem-specific source options.
- [Scan](https://docs.rs/struct.ScanError.html)- Error
- A scan-level error: a file that could not be validated at all.
- [Validation](https://docs.rs/struct.ValidationConfig.html)- Config
- Core validation config — applies regardless of input source.
- [Validation](https://docs.rs/struct.ValidationError.html)- Error
- A single validation error found in a documentation/config file.
- [Validation](https://docs.rs/struct.ValidationReport.html)- Report
- Result of a validation run.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Discovery](https://docs.rs/enum.DiscoveryMode.html)- Mode
- Controls how GTS identifier candidates are discovered in markdown files.
- [Scan](https://docs.rs/enum.ScanErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind
- The kind of scan-level failure that prevented a file from being validated.
- [Vendor](https://docs.rs/enum.VendorPolicy.html)- Policy
- Vendor matching policy for GTS ID validation.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_fs.html)- fs
- Validate GTS identifiers in files on disk.

# rite_tui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rite-tui/0.3.1/rite_tui/

## Expand description

Interactive terminal frontend for Rite ceremonies, built on
[ ratatui](https://docs.rs/ratatui/0.30.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/ratatui/index.html) and shaped as a TEA (The Elm Architecture) application.

The crate exposes a single entry point, [ run](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html), that the CLI invokes
after spawning the executor thread. Inside, the loop merges three
input sources into a single

[stream:](https://docs.rs/enum.Msg.html)

`Msg`- keyboard / resize events from `crossterm`
- executor events from the runtime channel
- timer ticks for spinner animation

`update(model, msg)` is pure and the only place state changes; it
returns a list of [ Cmd](https://docs.rs/enum.Cmd.html)s the runtime interprets (sending commands
back to the executor, quitting).

`view(model, frame)` is pure and the
only place rendering happens.[§](https://docs.rs#stability)Stability

Internal crate. This is an implementation detail of the `rite` CLI, with no
stable API and no semver guarantees across releases. Build against the
public `rite-sdk`, `rite-model`, or `rite-resolver` crates instead.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Model](https://docs.rs/struct.Model.html)
- Top-level UI state. A single `Screen`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Cmd](https://docs.rs/enum.Cmd.html)
- Side effect produced by `update``update`call.
- [Msg](https://docs.rs/enum.Msg.html)
- Input to the pure `update`
- [Running](https://docs.rs/enum.RunningState.html)- State
- Lifecycle phase of the ceremony as observed by the UI.
- [Screen](https://docs.rs/enum.Screen.html)
- Single source of truth for which screen is visible. Because only one variant is active at a time, we can’t render two contradictory views or sit “in a modal over a different modal”, exactly one screen, always.
- [StepTab](https://docs.rs/enum.StepTab.html)
- Active tab on the main screen.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [run](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html)
- Drive the TUI against a pair of runtime channels.

---

# rite 0.3.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rite/0.3.1

# rite

Author, execute, and verify cryptographic key ceremonies from the command line.

Ceremonies are written in a YAML DSL. `rite` validates them (`rite check`), produces the printable protocol participants follow (`rite script`), guides operators and witnesses through execution while recording an append-only transcript (`rite run`), and confirms and reports on the result (`rite verify`, `rite report`).

See the [main repository](https://github.com/rite-ly/rite) for installation, documentation, and examples.

---

# num_bigint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-bigint/0.4.7/num_bigint/

## Expand description

Big Integer Types for Rust

- A `BigUint`
- A `BigInt``BigUint``Sign`

Common numerical operations are overloaded, so we can treat them the same way we treat other numbers.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_bigint::BigUint;
use num_traits::One;
// Calculate large fibonacci numbers.
fn fib(n: usize) -> BigUint {
    let mut f0 = BigUint::ZERO;
    let mut f1 = BigUint::ONE;
    for _ in 0..n {
        let f2 = f0 + &f1;
        f0 = f1;
        f1 = f2;
    }
    f0
}
// This is a very large number.
println!("fib(1000) = {}", fib(1000));
```
It’s easy to generate large random numbers:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use num_bigint::{ToBigInt, RandBigInt};
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let a = rng.gen_bigint(1000);
let low = -10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let high = 10000.to_bigint().unwrap();
let b = rng.gen_bigint_range(&low, &high);
// Probably an even larger number.
println!("{}", a * b);
```
See the “Features” section for instructions for enabling random number generation.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

The `std` crate feature is enabled by default, which enables [ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html)
implementations and some internal use of floating point approximations. This can be disabled by
depending on

`num-bigint` with `default-features = false`. Either way, the `alloc` crate is
always required for heap allocation of the [/](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[digits.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#random-generation)Random Generation

`num-bigint` supports the generation of random big integers when the `rand`
feature is enabled. To enable it include rand as

```
rand = "0.8"
num-bigint = { version = "0.4", features = ["rand"] }
```
Note that you must use the version of `rand` that `num-bigint` is compatible
with: `0.8`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arbitrary-big-integers)Arbitrary Big Integers

`num-bigint` supports `arbitrary` and `quickcheck` features to implement
[ arbitrary::Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/1.4.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html) and

[, respectively, for both](https://docs.rs/quickcheck/1.0.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/quickcheck/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`quickcheck::Arbitrary`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[. These are useful for fuzzing and other forms of randomized testing.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

The `serde` feature adds implementations of [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) and

[for both](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[. Their serialized data is generated portably, regardless of platform differences like the internal digit size.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

The `num-bigint` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)
- A big signed integer type.
- [BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)
- A big unsigned integer type.
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/struct.ParseBigIntError.html)- BigInt - Error
- [Random](https://docs.rs/struct.RandomBits.html)- Bits - `rand`
- A random distribution for `BigUint``BigInt`
- [TryFrom](https://docs.rs/struct.TryFromBigIntError.html)- BigInt - Error
- The error type returned when a checked conversion regarding big integer fails.
- [U32Digits](https://docs.rs/struct.U32Digits.html)
- An iterator of `u32`digits representation of a`BigUint``BigInt`
- [U64Digits](https://docs.rs/struct.U64Digits.html)
- An iterator of `u64`digits representation of a`BigUint``BigInt`
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformBigInt.html)- BigInt - `rand`
- The back-end implementing rand’s `UniformSampler``BigInt`
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformBigUint.html)- BigUint - `rand`
- The back-end implementing rand’s `UniformSampler``BigUint`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Rand](https://docs.rs/trait.RandBigInt.html)- BigInt - `rand`
- A trait for sampling random big integers.
- [ToBig](https://docs.rs/trait.ToBigInt.html)- Int
- A generic trait for converting a value to a `BigInt``None`when converting from`f32`or`f64`, and will always succeed when converting from any integer or unsigned primitive, or`BigUint`
- [ToBig](https://docs.rs/trait.ToBigUint.html)- Uint
- A generic trait for converting a value to a `BigUint`

# rite_stdlib - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rite-stdlib/0.3.1/rite_stdlib/

## Expand description

Standard action library for Rite ceremonies.

This crate provides the built-in action implementations:

- **Verification**:- `clock_check`,- `confirm`,- `check_value`,- `oral_readback`,- `machine_info`
- **Attestation**:- `attest`
- **Crypto**:- `generate_keypair`,- `export_public`,- `wrap_key`,- `unwrap_key`
- **PKI**:- `generate_csr`,- `issue_certificate`

[§](https://docs.rs#backend-integration)Backend integration

All crypto and PKI actions require a backend; there are no software
fallbacks. For dry-run mode, configure a `MockBackend` in your
ceremony YAML.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `verification`: verification actions (requires- `subtle`,- `sysinfo`)
- `attestation`: attestation recording
- `crypto`: crypto actions (- `generate_keypair`,- `export_public`,- `wrap_key`,- `unwrap_key`)
- `pki`: PKI actions (- `generate_csr`,- `issue_certificate`; requires- `x509-cert`,- `der`,- `sha1`,- `rsa`,- `p256`)
- `default`: all features enabled

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

```
use rite_stdlib::default_registry;
let registry = default_registry();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#stability)Stability

Internal crate. This is an implementation detail of the `rite` CLI, with no
stable API and no semver guarantees across releases. Build against the
public `rite-sdk`, `rite-model`, or `rite-resolver` crates instead.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use backend::`- [MockBackend](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.MockBackend.html);
- `pub use backend::`- [create_backend](https://docs.rs/backend/fn.create_backend.html);
- `pub use backend::`- [default_backend_factory](https://docs.rs/backend/fn.default_backend_factory.html);
- `pub use attestation::`- [AttestAction](https://docs.rs/attestation/struct.AttestAction.html);
- `pub use crypto::`- [ExportPublicAction](https://docs.rs/crypto/struct.ExportPublicAction.html);

# rite_render - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rite-render/0.3.1/rite_render/

## Expand description

Document generation for Rite ceremonies.

- `script`: printable HTML briefing produced from a resolved- `rite_model::Ceremony`- `rite script`).
- `report`: post-ceremony HTML report produced from a verified- `StepFact`transcript (consumed by- `rite report`).

Rendering uses embedded [minijinja](https://docs.rs/minijinja) templates with a built-in theme
selected via [ Theme](https://docs.rs/enum.Theme.html), and optional run-time

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Branding.html)

`Branding`[§](https://docs.rs#stability)Stability

Internal crate. This is an implementation detail of the `rite` CLI, with no
stable API and no semver guarantees across releases. Build against the
public `rite-sdk`, `rite-model`, or `rite-resolver` crates instead.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A group of sections belonging to one act.
- [Branding](https://docs.rs/struct.Branding.html)
- Optional run-time branding applied on top of any built-in theme.
- [Report](https://docs.rs/struct.ReportView.html)- View
- Top-level context for the post-ceremony report templates.
- [Script](https://docs.rs/struct.ScriptStructure.html)- Structure
- Organized ceremony structure for script generation.
- [Script](https://docs.rs/struct.ScriptView.html)- View
- Top-level context for the ceremony script templates.
- [Section](https://docs.rs/struct.SectionGroup.html)- Group
- A group of steps belonging to one section.

- Render a ceremony script to a self-contained HTML document.

- `$ref`resolution for registered GTS schemas: inlining- `gts://`and local- `#/`references into a self-contained body. A- `$ref`target is inlined at a non-root position, so its root-only keys (- `$id`/- `$schema`and the- `x-gts-*`type-level modifiers) are stripped on the way in.- `allOf`and the other combinators are preserved verbatim — composition is left to the JSON Schema validator, not flattened here.

# rite_openssl - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rite-openssl/0.3.1/rite_openssl/

## Expand description

OpenSSL backend for Rite ceremonies.

Provides [ OpenSslBackend](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenSslBackend.html), a software cryptographic backend backed by OpenSSL.
Keys are held in memory for the lifetime of the backend instance.

[§](https://docs.rs#capabilities)Capabilities

[ OpenSslBackend](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenSslBackend.html) implements the following

[traits:](https://docs.rs/rite-sdk/0.3.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rite_sdk/index.html)

`rite_sdk`- `KeyStoreBackend`
- `SignBackend`
- `KeyTransportBackend`
- `RandomBackend`

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

- `vendored`: bundle OpenSSL at build time (no system library needed). Required for air-gapped USB image builds.

[§](https://docs.rs#stability)Stability

Internal crate. This is an implementation detail of the `rite` CLI, with no
stable API and no semver guarantees across releases. Build against the
public `rite-sdk`, `rite-model`, or `rite-resolver` crates instead.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenSslBackend.html)- SslBackend
- OpenSSL-based cryptographic backend.

# rite_runtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rite-runtime/0.3.1/rite_runtime/

## Expand description

Execution runtime for Rite ceremonies.

`rite-runtime` defines the protocol that frontends use to drive a
ceremony to completion, the executor that walks the ceremony plan,
and the supporting machinery for transcripts and action handlers.

[§](https://docs.rs#key-types)Key types

- `Executor`
- `Action`- `ActionRegistry`
- `BackendRegistry`- `BackendFactory`
- `Reporter`
- `TranscriptSink`

[§](https://docs.rs#stability)Stability

Internal crate. This is an implementation detail of the `rite` CLI, with no
stable API and no semver guarantees across releases. Build against the
public `rite-sdk`, `rite-model`, or `rite-resolver` crates instead.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_support/index.html)- support
- Test-only helpers for action implementors.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Action](https://docs.rs/struct.ActionMetadata.html)- Metadata
- Metadata describing an action, used for validation and presentation.
- [Action](https://docs.rs/struct.ActionRegistry.html)- Registry
- Registry mapping action types to their handlers.
- [Backend](https://docs.rs/struct.BackendRegistry.html)- Registry
- Backend registry that owns all backend lifecycle state.
- [Backend](https://docs.rs/struct.BackendVersion.html)- Version
- A linked cryptographic backend library and its runtime version.
- [Build](https://docs.rs/struct.BuildInfo.html)- Info
- Identity of the running `rite`binary. A property of the artifact, set at compile time; the strongly verifiable end of the trust boundary (checkable against a release tag and build provenance).
- [Ceremony](https://docs.rs/struct.CeremonyRandom.html)- Random
- The per-ceremony entropy source.
- [Disk](https://docs.rs/struct.Disk.html)
- A block device and its mount, as shown in the System tab.
- [Draw](https://docs.rs/struct.Draw.html)
- A value drawn from the source, paired with the path that derives it.
- [Entropy](https://docs.rs/struct.EntropyVerified.html)- Verified
- Outcome of re-deriving a transcript’s entropy source.
- [Environment](https://docs.rs/struct.Environment.html)
- Live inventory of the machine’s attached devices.

- Complete execution state, recreated after each step.

- Summary returned by `Executor::run`

- Channel-driven executor. One per ceremony run.

optional human context. Replaces the free-form status strings the
`machine_info`action used to emit.
- [Handler](https://docs.rs/struct.HandlerContext.html)- Context
- Read-only view of execution state for handlers.
- [Hardening](https://docs.rs/struct.Hardening.html)
- Snapshot of platform memory- and DMA-protection features.
- [Host](https://docs.rs/struct.HostInfo.html)- Info
- Identity of the host machine. A property of the environment, the weakly verifiable end of the trust boundary (an operator assertion that software can only partly corroborate).
- [InMemory](https://docs.rs/struct.InMemorySink.html)- Sink
- In-memory sink that collects every recorded `StepFact`

- JSONL file sink with SHA-256 chain integrity.
- [Loaded](https://docs.rs/struct.LoadedTranscript.html)- Transcript
- Verified transcript contents, chain-walked facts plus the final fingerprint and a flag for whether the run reached a terminal fact.
- [Material](https://docs.rs/struct.MaterialOverview.html)- Overview

- [Output](https://docs.rs/struct.OutputConfig.html)- Config
- Configuration for ceremony output directory structure.
- [Prompt](https://docs.rs/struct.PromptId.html)- Id
- Identifier that pairs a prompt request with its matching response.
- [Reporter](https://docs.rs/struct.Reporter.html)
- Action-facing handle threaded into every action handler.
- [Startup](https://docs.rs/struct.StartupSnapshot.html)- Snapshot
- The one-shot UI snapshots emitted at ceremony start: static system identity and the initial device environment.
- [Step](https://docs.rs/struct.StepInfo.html)- Info
- Information about a step needed by action handlers.
- [Step](https://docs.rs/struct.StepResult.html)- Result
- Result of executing a step.

- [Timed](https://docs.rs/struct.TimedFact.html)- Fact

by `read_verified_transcript`

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DERIVATION_](https://docs.rs/constant.DERIVATION_V1.html)- V1
- Frozen-scheme tag recorded with the machine seed. It pins the *entire*construction (Extract/Expand, the ratchet rule, the`info`/path byte encodings), not merely the hash. A verifier treats it as a selector among known-good schemes it already trusts and rejects any value it does not recognise, it is never an instruction to trust an arbitrary algorithm.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_DRAW_LEN.html)- DRAW_ - LEN
- Longest value a single draw can produce: the `HKDF-Expand`output limit of`255 * HashLen`bytes (RFC 5869), with SHA-256’s 32-byte output. [`expand`] panics beyond this, so anything replaying a recorded draw must bound the requested length by this value first.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Action](https://docs.rs/trait.Action.html)
- Action trait, every ceremony step handler implements this.
- [Clock](https://docs.rs/trait.Clock.html)
- Source of wall-clock time for a ceremony run.
- [Transcript](https://docs.rs/trait.TranscriptSink.html)- Sink
- Synchronous, durable observer of `StepFact`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_path.html)- path
- Build a derivation path. The single place the path format lives, so the
draw side and the verify side cannot drift. A `purpose`is drawn at most once per step, so`(epoch, step, purpose)`uniquely identifies a value.
- [compute_](https://docs.rs/fn.compute_file_fingerprint.html)- file_ - fingerprint
- SHA-256 fingerprint of a file’s contents.
- [compute_](https://docs.rs/fn.compute_fingerprint.html)- fingerprint
- SHA-256 fingerprint of an in-memory byte slice.
- [derive_](https://docs.rs/fn.derive_value.html)- value
- Derive the value at `path`from the given epoch seed.
- [evaluate](https://docs.rs/fn.evaluate.html)
- Evaluate an expression in the given context.
- [evaluate_](https://docs.rs/fn.evaluate_expr_value.html)- expr_ - value
- Evaluate an `ExprValue`to a JSON value.
- [evaluate_](https://docs.rs/fn.evaluate_expr_value_to_string.html)- expr_ - value_ - to_ - string
- Evaluate an `ExprValue`to a string.
- [fact_](https://docs.rs/fn.fact_summary.html)- summary
- One-line summary of a `StepFact`
- [fold_](https://docs.rs/fn.fold_seed.html)- seed
- Advance the ratchet by one epoch, folding in a human contribution.
- [initial_](https://docs.rs/fn.initial_seed.html)- seed
- Compute `seed_0`from the machine entropy`m`.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_params.html)- params
- Deserialize the per-step parameter blob into a typed handler-specific struct.
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_verified_transcript.html)- verified_ - transcript
- Verify a JSONL transcript and return its facts.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_artifact_bytes.html)- artifact_ - bytes
- Resolve an artifact reference to byte content.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_backend_key.html)- backend_ - key
- Resolve an artifact to a backend-managed key reference.
- [signal_](https://docs.rs/fn.signal_summary.html)- summary
- One-line summary of a `UiSignal`
- [truncate_](https://docs.rs/fn.truncate_for_display.html)- for_ - display
- Truncate a string to at most `max_chars`Unicode scalar values, appending`"..."`when truncation occurs.
- [value_](https://docs.rs/fn.value_to_json.html)- to_ - json
- Convert a Value to a JSON value for action parameters.
- [verify_](https://docs.rs/fn.verify_entropy.html)- entropy
- Re-derive a transcript’s entropy source and confirm every drawn value.
- [verify_](https://docs.rs/fn.verify_step_fact_transcript.html)- step_ - fact_ - transcript
- Verify a JSONL transcript file produced by `JsonlFileSink`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Backend](https://docs.rs/type.BackendFactory.html)- Factory
- A closure that creates a concrete backend from its name and config.

# ordeal 0.3.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ordeal/0.3.0

# Ordeal

`ordeal` (meaning "verdict / judgment") is a specialized,
**certificate-checked** QF_BV SMT solver for the [PulseEngine](https://github.com/pulseengine) toolchain. It
exists to replace the Z3 static-link build pain that loom (verified WASM
optimizer) and synth (verified WASM→ARM codegen) carry today — grounding:
loom issue #246.

## Design in one paragraph

An **untrusted solver** emits a machine-checkable **LRAT UNSAT
certificate**; a small **formally-verified checker** validates it. Only the
checker is trusted (the CompCert certifying-algorithm pattern; blueprint =
Lean 4 `bv_decide`, OOPSLA 2025). Z3 is demoted to a differential *oracle*
and benchmark *rival*, not the production engine. The pipeline is: term
graph → bit-blast → AIG → CNF (Tseitin) → SAT → LRAT → verified checker.

## Modules

- [`term`] — the closed QF_BV fragment (the exact loom #246 op set).
- [`solver`] — the one-shot`check-sat`interface and result types.
- [`eval`] — the concrete evaluator (executable SMT-LIB semantics; the test oracle for every blasting rule and the SAT-model self-check).
- [`aig`] — the And-Inverter Graph arena (structural hashing, folding).
- [`blast`] — per-op-family bit-blasting rules (term → AIG).
- [`cnf`] — CNF types and the Tseitin encoder (AIG → CNF).
- [`sat`] — the pure-Rust CDCL core (primary engine on every target).
- [`lrat`] — LRAT certificate emission from the CDCL proof trace; the`ordeal-lrat`crate (the sole trusted component) validates it before any`Unsat`is returned.
- [`oracle`] — the Z3 differential oracle (behind the`oracle`feature).

---

# ordeal_lrat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal-lrat/^0.3.0/

## Expand description

Ordeal’s LRAT certificate checker — **the sole trusted component**.

The ordeal solver is untrusted: an `Unsat` answer is believed only when
this checker has validated an LRAT certificate for it. This crate is
written to be translated to Lean 4 (via Aeneas) and formally verified, so
everything here is deliberately small, simple, and obviously correct:
no `unsafe`, no dependencies, no cleverness.

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-dialect-textual-lrat-rup-only)Supported dialect: textual LRAT, **RUP-only**

**LOUD LIMITATION:** this checker supports only RUP (Reverse Unit
Propagation) addition steps. RAT steps — recognised by *negative* clause
ids in the hint list — are **rejected** with
[ CheckError::RatUnsupported](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckError.html#variant.RatUnsupported). This is deliberate: ordeal’s CDCL engine
emits RUP-only proofs, and rejecting is always sound (we may refuse a
valid certificate, we never accept an invalid one).

Accepted line forms (whitespace-separated integers, one step per line;
blank lines and lines starting with `c` are skipped as comments):

- Addition: `<id> <lit>* 0 <hint>* 0`— adds the clause`<lit>*`with id`<id>`, justified by unit propagation through the clauses named by`<hint>*`, in order.
- Deletion: `<id> d <id>* 0`— marks the named clauses dead. The leading`<id>`is informational (as emitted by drat-trim) and is not checked.

Clause ids are 1-based: original clause `i` of the input CNF (0-based)
has id `i + 1`; each addition step must then use exactly the next
sequential id (this is what ordeal emits; sparse ids are rejected).

[§](https://docs.rs#what-checked-means)What “checked” means

An addition step `C` with hints `h1..hk` is verified by assuming the
negation of every literal of `C` and then unit-propagating through the
hint clauses in order: each hint must be either *falsified* (conflict —
the step is verified, so CNF ∧ ¬C is unsat, i.e. CNF ⊨ C) or *unit*
(its single unassigned literal is assigned true). Anything else —
a satisfied hint, a hint with two or more unassigned literals, running
out of hints, a dead or unknown id — rejects the certificate.

The whole certificate is accepted iff it parses in full AND some verified
addition step adds the **empty clause** (checking stops at that step;
parsed trailing steps are ignored). Parsing everything first is stricter
than strictly necessary and always sound (extra rejections only).

[§](https://docs.rs#structure-parser-vs-kernel)Structure: parser vs kernel

The crate is split for the formal proof (issue #12): the [ kernel](https://docs.rs/kernel/index.html)
module is the string-free checking core — the Aeneas → Lean translation
target carrying the soundness theorem — and this file is the untrusted
text parser feeding it. The CNF reaches the kernel directly, so parser
bugs cannot manufacture an acceptance (see

`kernel` docs).## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [kernel](https://docs.rs/kernel/index.html)
- The string-free checking core — **the Aeneas → Lean translation target**.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Check](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckError.html)- Error
- Why a certificate was rejected (or could not even be read).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check](https://docs.rs/fn.check.html)
- Check a textual LRAT `certificate`against the input`cnf`.

# z3 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/z3/^0.20.2/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#z3)Z3

Z3 is a theorem prover [from Microsoft Research](https://github.com/Z3Prover/z3/).

This library aims to provide an idiomatic Rust wrapper around Z3.

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage)Basic Usage

The simplest way to use Z3 is to build a formula (also known as an [ Ast](https://docs.rs/ast/trait.Ast.html))
and use Z3’s

[to find solutions to it.](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html)

`Solver`This example walks through the process of expressing a simple math problem in the language of SMT, asserting it into a Solver, and extracting answers from it. Z3 can encode much more varied and complex problems than this example shows (and some of these features are supported by the Rust bindings), but this covers the absolute basics.

Consider the following problem:

Three friends, named Alice, Bob, and Charlie, wish to divide 30 apples amongst themselves, subject to the following constraints:

- Everyone must get at least one apple.
- All apples must be accounted for.
- Alice must receive at least 5 apples.
- Bob must receive an even number of apples.
- Charlie must get at least as many apples as Bob.
- The number of apples Alice receives must be exactly 3 times more than the number Charlie receives.
What are the possible distributions of apples they could make?

To express this in Z3, we define symbolic `Int`[ Ast](https://docs.rs/ast/trait.Ast.html)s representing the number
of apples each friend has, and

[the constraints of the problem into a](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html#method.assert)

`assert`[. We can then query the](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html)

`Solver`[for a solution:](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html)

`Solver````
 // define Int values representing the number of apples each friend has
 let alice = Int::fresh_const("alice");
 let bob = Int::fresh_const("bob");
 let charlie = Int::fresh_const("charlie");
 // instantiate a Solver
 let solver = Solver::new();
 // encode the constraints of the problem as Bool-valued Asts
 // and assert them in the solver
 solver.assert((&alice + &bob + &charlie).eq(30));
 solver.assert(alice.gt(0));
 solver.assert(bob.gt(0));
 solver.assert(charlie.gt(0));
 solver.assert(alice.ge(5));
 solver.assert((&bob % 2).eq(0));
 solver.assert(charlie.ge(&bob));
 solver.assert(alice.eq(&charlie * 3));
 // iterate over the solutions to our variables
 for solution in solver
     .solutions([alice, bob, charlie], false)
     // we use take to ensure that this loop terminates in case there are very many solutions
     .take(100) {
     // extract concrete values for each modeled Int Ast
     let solution: Vec<u64> = solution.iter().map(Int::as_u64).map(Option::unwrap).collect();
     let alice = solution[0];
     let bob = solution[1];
     let charlie = solution[2];
     println!("alice: {alice}, bob: {bob}, charlie: {charlie}");
     // check that the concrete values match the constraints we gave the solver
     assert_eq!(alice + bob + charlie, 30);
     assert!(alice >= 5);
     assert_eq!(bob % 2, 0);
     assert!(charlie >= bob);
     assert_eq!(alice, charlie * 3);
 }
```
In this case, there are 2 solutions, and the above snippet gives the following output:

`alice: 21, bob: 2, charlie: 7`

`alice: 18, bob: 6, charlie: 6`

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/src/ordeal/lib.rs.html

# ordeal/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! # Ordeal
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! `ordeal` (meaning "verdict / judgment") is a specialized,
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! **certificate-checked** QF_BV SMT solver for the [PulseEngine] toolchain. It
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! exists to replace the Z3 static-link build pain that loom (verified WASM
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! optimizer) and synth (verified WASM→ARM codegen) carry today — grounding:
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! loom issue #246.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! ## Design in one paragraph
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! An **untrusted solver** emits a machine-checkable **LRAT UNSAT
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! certificate**; a small **formally-verified checker** validates it. Only the
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! checker is trusted (the CompCert certifying-algorithm pattern; blueprint =
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! Lean 4 `bv_decide`, OOPSLA 2025). Z3 is demoted to a differential *oracle*
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! and benchmark *rival*, not the production engine. The pipeline is: term
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! graph → bit-blast → AIG → CNF (Tseitin) → SAT → LRAT → verified checker.
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! ## Modules
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! - [`term`] — the closed QF_BV fragment (the exact loom #246 op set).
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! - [`solver`] — the one-shot `check-sat` interface and result types.
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! - [`eval`] — the concrete evaluator (executable SMT-LIB semantics; the
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!   test oracle for every blasting rule and the SAT-model self-check).
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! - [`aig`] — the And-Inverter Graph arena (structural hashing, folding).
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! - [`blast`] — per-op-family bit-blasting rules (term → AIG).
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! - [`cnf`] — CNF types and the Tseitin encoder (AIG → CNF).
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! - [`sat`] — the pure-Rust CDCL core (primary engine on every target).
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! - [`lrat`] — LRAT certificate emission from the CDCL proof trace; the
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!   `ordeal-lrat` crate (the sole trusted component) validates it before
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!   any `Unsat` is returned.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! - [`oracle`] — the Z3 differential oracle (behind the `oracle` feature).
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! [PulseEngine]: https://github.com/pulseengine
[34](https://docs.rs#34)
[35](https://docs.rs#35)pub mod aig;
[36](https://docs.rs#36)pub mod blast;
[37](https://docs.rs#37)pub mod cnf;
[38](https://docs.rs#38)pub mod eval;
[39](https://docs.rs#39)pub mod lrat;
[40](https://docs.rs#40)pub mod sat;
[41](https://docs.rs#41)pub mod sliver;
[42](https://docs.rs#42)pub mod solver;
[43](https://docs.rs#43)pub mod term;
[44](https://docs.rs#44)
[45](https://docs.rs#45)#[cfg(feature = "oracle")]
[46](https://docs.rs#46)pub mod oracle;
[47](https://docs.rs#47)
[48](https://docs.rs#48)pub use solver::{Certificate, CheckResult, Model, Solver};
[49](https://docs.rs#49)pub use term::{BoolTerm, BvTerm, Sort};

# ordeal::term - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/ordeal/term/index.html

## Expand description

The `ordeal` term language: the closed QF_BV fragment from loom issue #246.

This module defines the **exact, closed** set of operations `ordeal` is
designed to decide. It is deliberately small: `ordeal` is not a general
SMT solver but a specialized decision procedure for the equivalence and
satisfiability queries that loom (verified WASM optimizer) and synth
(verified WASM→ARM codegen) actually emit.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-fragment-qf_bv-widths-8--32--64)The fragment (QF_BV, widths 8 / 32 / 64)

- **Bitvector ops:**- `bvadd`,- `bvsub`,- `bvmul`,- `bvudiv`,- `bvand`,- `bvor`,- `bvxor`,- `bvshl`,- `bvlshr`,- `bvashr`,- `bvrotr`,- `extract{hi,lo}`,- `concat`,- `zero_ext{by}`,- `sign_ext{by}`.
- **Boolean predicates**(what you assert / check):- `eq`,- `ne`,- `ult`,- `ule`,- `ugt`,- `uge`,- `slt`,- `sle`,- `sgt`,- `sge`, plus- `not`/- `and`/- `or`over booleans.

A query is one-shot `check-sat` expecting **UNSAT** (equivalence holds),
returning a **counterexample model** when SAT.

[§](https://docs.rs#explicitly-out-of-scope)Explicitly out of scope

Quantifiers, floating-point, `Optimize`, and incremental solving are NOT
in scope and MUST NOT be added here. Adding an operation outside this set
silently widens the trusted fragment — do not do it.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Sort](https://docs.rs/struct.Sort.html)
- A bitvector sort, parameterized by bit width.

---

# ordeal::solver - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/ordeal/solver/index.html

## Expand description

The one-shot solver interface and the P1 pipeline dispatcher (DES-012).

Callers (loom, synth) build a conjunction of asserted [ BoolTerm](https://docs.rs/term/enum.BoolTerm.html)s and call

[. The result is one of:](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html#method.check)

`Solver::check`- `CheckResult::Unsat`- `Certificate`
- `CheckResult::Sat`- `Model`- **self-checked**by re-evaluating it against every assertion with the concrete evaluator.
- `CheckResult::Unknown`

[§](https://docs.rs#soundness-contract-for-callers)Soundness contract for callers

`Unknown` MUST be treated **conservatively**: loom/synth must NOT apply the
optimization / accept the codegen when they receive `Unknown`. Only a
checked `Unsat` certificate authorizes a transformation.

[§](https://docs.rs#pipeline-status-p2-certificate-checked)Pipeline status (P2: certificate-checked)

`check` runs blast → AIG → Tseitin CNF → CDCL. On SAT it returns a
self-checked model. On UNSAT the LRAT certificate emitted from the CDCL
proof trace is validated by the `ordeal-lrat` checker **before** `Unsat`
is returned — an `Unsat` the checker did not accept degrades to `Unknown`
(AGENTS.md rule 1: no unchecked `Unsat`, ever). The raw engine verdict is
exposed crate-internally for the differential oracle only.

Trust status: the checker is small, dependency-free, and mutation-tested; its formal soundness proof (Rust → Lean 4 via Aeneas, TR-013) is the remaining P2 obligation and is tracked in rivet as FEAT-002.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-op-enablement-gate-p1-kill-criterion)The op-enablement gate (P1 kill criterion)

Every operation’s blasting rule ships oracle-verified (UV-005..UV-009).
If the differential oracle ever finds a disagreement, that op is added to
[`DISABLED_OPS`] and every query containing it returns `Unknown` until
the rule is fixed — the solver reverts to conservative, never guesses.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Certificate](https://docs.rs/struct.Certificate.html)
- A machine-checkable UNSAT certificate.
- [Model](https://docs.rs/struct.Model.html)
- A satisfying assignment (counterexample) for a SAT query.
- [Solver](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html)
- A one-shot QF_BV solver over the closed loom #246 fragment.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Check](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckResult.html)- Result
- The verdict of a one-shot `check`.
- [OpKind](https://docs.rs/enum.OpKind.html)
- Every operation in the closed fragment, for the enablement gate.

# ordeal::eval - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/ordeal/eval/index.html

## Expand description

Concrete evaluator for the closed QF_BV fragment — the executable SMT-LIB semantics (DES-001).

This is the **test oracle** for every bit-blasting rule (exhaustive at
width 8, randomized at 32/64) and the SAT-model self-check: a returned
model is re-evaluated here before `check` reports `Sat`.

Values are `u128` masked to the term width. Widths are arbitrary in
1..=128 *inside* a term (an `extract` produces narrow intermediates);
the 8/32/64 restriction applies to the variables loom/synth declare.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Eval](https://docs.rs/enum.EvalError.html)- Error
- Why evaluation (or sort-checking) failed.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [bv_sort](https://docs.rs/fn.bv_sort.html)
- Compute the sort (width) of a term, checking well-sortedness.
- [eval_](https://docs.rs/fn.eval_bool.html)- bool
- Evaluate a boolean term (predicate / connective) to a concrete truth value.
- [eval_bv](https://docs.rs/fn.eval_bv.html)
- Evaluate a bitvector term to its concrete value (masked to its width).

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Env](https://docs.rs/type.Env.html)
- A variable assignment: name → concrete value (masked to the var’s width).

# ordeal::aig - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/ordeal/aig/index.html

## Expand description

And-Inverter Graph with structural hashing and constant folding (DES-002).

AIGER literal convention: a [ Lit](https://docs.rs/struct.Lit.html) is

`variable << 1 | complement`.
Variable 0 is the constant, so `Lit(0)` is FALSE and `Lit(1)` is TRUE.
Inputs and AND nodes occupy consecutive variable indices in one arena.The [ Aig::and](https://docs.rs/struct.Aig.html#method.and) constructor folds constants (

`x&0=0`, `x&1=x`, `x&x=x`,
`x&!x=0`) and structurally hashes operand-normalized pairs, so common
subexpressions collapse before the CNF stage ever sees them.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [word_](https://docs.rs/fn.word_const.html)- const
- A constant word of the given width.
- [word_](https://docs.rs/fn.word_input.html)- input
- A word of fresh inputs.
- [word_](https://docs.rs/fn.word_value.html)- value
- Decode a simulated word back to a value (LSB first).

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Word](https://docs.rs/type.Word.html)
- A bitvector as AIG literals, **LSB first**(`word[0]`is bit 0).

---

# ordeal::blast - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/ordeal/blast/index.html

## Expand description

Bit-blasting rules: each QF_BV operation lowered to AIG gates (DES-005..DES-009), one module per op family.

Words are LSB-first [ Word](https://docs.rs/aig/type.Word.html)s. Every rule is verified
against the concrete evaluator (DES-001): exhaustively at width 8,
randomized at widths 32/64. A rule that has not passed its UV measure is
not enabled in the pipeline (the P1 kill criterion).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [arith](https://docs.rs/arith/index.html)
- Add/sub and the eight ordered comparisons (DES-006).
- [bitwise](https://docs.rs/bitwise/index.html)
- Bitwise ops and (dis)equality (DES-005): bvand, bvor, bvxor, eq, ne.
- [muldiv](https://docs.rs/muldiv/index.html)
- Multiplication and unsigned division (DES-008): shift-add partial products; restoring long division with the SMT-LIB divide-by-zero case (divisor = 0 ⇒ all-ones quotient) merged via a divisor-is-zero mux.
- [shift](https://docs.rs/shift/index.html)
- Shifts and rotate (DES-007): barrel shifter with SMT-LIB out-of-range semantics; bvrotr rotates by amount mod width.
- [structural](https://docs.rs/structural/index.html)
- Structural ops (DES-009): extract, concat, zero_ext, sign_ext. Pure word plumbing — no gates.

---

# ordeal::cnf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/ordeal/cnf/index.html

## Expand description

CNF representation and the Tseitin encoder (DES-003).

Literals are DIMACS-style nonzero `i32`s: positive means the variable is
asserted true, negative means false. Variables are numbered from 1.

[ tseitin](https://docs.rs/fn.tseitin.html) lowers an

[to an equisatisfiable CNF in linear size: CNF variable](https://docs.rs/aig/struct.Aig.html)

`Aig``v+1` corresponds to AIG variable `v` (the +1 skips DIMACS
variable 0), three clauses per AND gate, the constant node pinned false,
and one unit clause per asserted output literal.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [CnfFormula](https://docs.rs/struct.CnfFormula.html)
- A CNF formula.
- [Tseitin](https://docs.rs/struct.TseitinMap.html)- Map
- The AIG-variable → CNF-variable correspondence produced by `tseitin`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [tseitin](https://docs.rs/fn.tseitin.html)
- Tseitin-transform the AIG, asserting every literal in `outputs`.

# ordeal::sat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/ordeal/sat/index.html

## Expand description

The pure-Rust CDCL SAT core (DES-004) — primary engine on every target.

Implements the classic conflict-driven clause-learning loop: two-watched- literal propagation, first-UIP conflict analysis with clause learning, VSIDS-style decision activities with phase saving, and Luby-sequence restarts (conflict-counter based — no wall clock, so the engine runs unchanged on wasm32-wasip2 and is fully deterministic). Learned clauses are never deleted, which also keeps proof-trace indices stable.

[§](https://docs.rs#proof-trace-the-p2-lrat-hook-tr-005)Proof trace (the P2 LRAT hook, TR-005)

Every learned clause is recorded as a [ LearnedStep](https://docs.rs/struct.LearnedStep.html) carrying the
antecedent clauses used in its conflict-analysis resolution. Antecedent
indices refer to the combined original+learned clause sequence: index

`i < n` is `formula.clauses[i]` exactly as passed to [(tautologies and duplicate literals included, so original indices line up one-to-one with the input), and index](https://docs.rs/struct.SatSolver.html#method.solve)

`SatSolver::solve``n + k` is the clause of the `k`-th
[, where](https://docs.rs/struct.LearnedStep.html)

`LearnedStep``n = formula.clauses.len()`.The antecedents of each step form a reverse-unit-propagation (RUP) chain:
assume the negation of every literal in `clause`, then process the
antecedents in order — each becomes unit (propagate its remaining
literal) until the last, which becomes falsified. Concretely the order is
root-level (level-0) unit reasons in assignment order, then the first-UIP
resolution reasons in trail order, then the conflicting clause last. When
the result is [ SatResult::Unsat](https://docs.rs/enum.SatResult.html#variant.Unsat) the final step’s

`clause` is empty:
that step records the derivation of the empty clause.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Learned](https://docs.rs/struct.LearnedStep.html)- Step
- One clause-learning step of the resolution proof (see module docs for
the indexing convention and the RUP ordering of `antecedents`).
- [SatSolver](https://docs.rs/struct.SatSolver.html)
- The CDCL solver.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [SatResult](https://docs.rs/enum.SatResult.html)
- The verdict of a SAT solve.

---

# ordeal::lrat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/ordeal/lrat/index.html

## Expand description

LRAT certificate emission from the CDCL proof trace (DES-013).

The CDCL core (DES-004) records every learned clause as a
[ LearnedStep](https://docs.rs/sat/struct.LearnedStep.html) whose antecedents already form a reverse-unit-propagation
chain, so emission is pure formatting into the textual LRAT dialect the

`ordeal-lrat` checker consumes:- the `k`-th learned step becomes addition line`n + k + 1`over`n`input clauses (ids strictly sequential, matching the checker);
- hints are the step’s antecedent indices, shifted to 1-based clause ids in their recorded RUP order;
- no deletion lines are emitted (the CDCL keeps learned clauses);
- an UNSAT trace ends with the empty-clause step, which is exactly the line that makes the checker accept.

The emitted certificate is UNTRUSTED output of an untrusted solver: the
pipeline (DES-013 wiring in `solver.rs`) returns `Unsat` only after the
checker accepts it.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [emit_](https://docs.rs/fn.emit_lrat.html)- lrat
- Format a proof trace as a textual LRAT certificate.

---

# Certificate in ordeal::solver - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/ordeal/solver/struct.Certificate.html

## Expand description

A machine-checkable UNSAT certificate.

The solver (untrusted) emits an LRAT proof; the `ordeal-lrat` checker
(the only trusted component) validated exactly these bytes before this
value was constructed. Callers can independently re-run
`ordeal_lrat::check` on them.

# Model in ordeal::solver - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/ordeal/solver/struct.Model.html

# Struct Model

[Source](../../src/ordeal/solver.rs.html#66-69) ```
pub struct Model {
    pub assignments:
```
[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html), [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u128.html))>,
}

## Expand description

# Solver in ordeal::solver - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/ordeal/solver/struct.Solver.html

`pub struct Solver { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A one-shot QF_BV solver over the closed loom #246 fragment.

Build up assertions with [ Solver::assert](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html#method.assert), then call

[. The solver is single-use in spirit (no incremental push/pop) matching the scope in](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html#method.check)

`Solver::check``README.md`.## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Add a boolean assertion to the conjunction to be checked.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/ordeal/solver.rs.html#398-410)

One-shot decision for an **extended (array/UF sliver) query**.

The sliver is eliminated into the closed QF_BV core by
[ crate::sliver::lower](https://docs.rs/sliver/fn.lower.html) — eager read-over-write for

`Array(BV32→BV8)`
select/store over concrete offsets, Ackermannization for
uninterpreted `pure_call` congruence — and the resulting pure
assertions are decided by the normal [pipeline.](https://docs.rs/struct.Solver.html#method.check)

`Solver::check`An **out-of-sliver** query (symbolic index, bad array sort, or an
inconsistent call signature — any [ crate::sliver::SliverError](https://docs.rs/sliver/enum.SliverError.html))
returns

[: conservative by construction, never a guess. Soundness is unchanged from](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckResult.html#variant.Unknown)

`CheckResult::Unknown``check` — no array/UF construct
ever reaches the bit-blaster; only the lowered core does.Check that every assertion is well-sorted, reporting the first
violation with a distinct error (TR-010). `check` treats ill-sorted
input as `Unknown`; this gives callers the actionable diagnosis.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/ordeal/solver.rs.html#430-446)#### pub fn [check](https://docs.rs#method.check)(&self) -> [CheckResult](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckResult.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/ordeal/solver.rs.html#430-446)

#### pub fn [check](https://docs.rs#method.check)(&self) -> [CheckResult](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckResult.html)

Decide satisfiability of the conjunction of all asserted terms.

Pipeline: blast → AIG → Tseitin CNF → CDCL. `Sat` carries a model
that has been re-evaluated against every assertion (self-check).
On engine-UNSAT the LRAT certificate emitted from the proof trace is
validated by the `ordeal-lrat` checker before `Unsat` is returned —
an `Unsat` the checker did not accept is never reported (it degrades
to `Unknown`, which is always sound).

# ordeal::sliver - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal/0.3.0/ordeal/sliver/index.html

## Expand description

The loom array/UF sliver (P3) — an extended query layer that is
**preprocessed away** into the closed QF_BV core before bit-blasting.

The core `term.rs` fragment stays closed (CLAUDE.md / loom #246): these
constructs have **no bit-blasting rule**. Instead they live in a separate
extended term language here and are eliminated by preprocessing
([ lower](https://docs.rs/fn.lower.html)) into a conjunction of plain

[assertions that the existing pipeline decides. No array/UF ops ever reach the AIG.](https://docs.rs/term/enum.BoolTerm.html)

`BoolTerm`What loom emits (ARCHITECTURE.md → “The array / UF sliver”, TR-008):

- **Non-extensional**modeling linear memory:- `Array(BV32 → BV8)`- `store`/- `select`over- **concrete consecutive offsets**only. No whole-array equality. Eliminated by- **eager read-over-write**: a- `select`on a- `store`chain reduces to a nested if-then-else over concrete index equalities down to the base array’s fresh per-index variables.
- **Uninterpreted**with- `pure_call`- **congruence**(same args ⇒ same result). Eliminated by- **Ackermannization**: each distinct call site becomes a fresh variable, plus congruence constraints- `args_i = args_j → result_i = result_j`across call sites of the same function.

Design decision (rivet DES-014): a separate `Ext*` layer rather than
widening `BvTerm`, so the core fragment’s “every op has a proven
bit-blasting rule” invariant is preserved by construction — the sliver
is sound *because* it never reaches the blaster, only the core does.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Lowered](https://docs.rs/struct.Lowered.html)
- The lowered core plus the provenance of every fresh variable it
introduced — the extra bookkeeping `lower`
- [Sliver](https://docs.rs/struct.SliverModel.html)- Model
- A concrete model for the extended language: the non-Z3 test oracle.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Array](https://docs.rs/enum.ArrayTerm.html)- Term
- An array-sorted term: `Array(BV32 → BV8)`, non-extensional.
- [ExtBool](https://docs.rs/enum.ExtBoolTerm.html)- Term
- A boolean-sorted term in the extended language.
- [ExtBv](https://docs.rs/enum.ExtBvTerm.html)- Term
- A bitvector-sorted term in the extended (sliver) language: the closed
core plus `select`and uninterpreted`pure_call`.
- [ExtOp](https://docs.rs/enum.ExtOp.html)
- The recursive core operations lifted over `ExtBvTerm`children. (One variant per`BvTerm`operator that has bitvector children; leaves —`Const`/`Var`— use`ExtBvTerm::Core`
- [Sliver](https://docs.rs/enum.SliverError.html)- Error
- Why a sliver query is outside the supported fragment.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- Eliminate the sliver into a pure-core conjunction (DES-014/015/016).
