# aes_gcm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aes-gcm/^0.10/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rustcrypto-aes-gcm)RustCrypto: AES-GCM

Pure Rust implementation of the AES-GCM
[Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authenticated_encryption) cipher.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-notes)Security Notes

This crate has received one [security audit by NCC Group](https://research.nccgroup.com/2020/02/26/public-report-rustcrypto-aes-gcm-and-chacha20poly1305-implementation-review/), with no significant
findings. We would like to thank [MobileCoin](https://www.mobilecoin.com/) for funding the audit.

All implementations contained in the crate are designed to execute in constant time, either by relying on hardware intrinsics (i.e. AES-NI and CLMUL on x86/x86_64), or using a portable implementation which is only constant time on processors which implement constant-time multiplication.

It is not suitable for use on processors with a variable-time multiplication operation (e.g. short circuit on multiply-by-zero / multiply-by-one, such as certain 32-bit PowerPC CPUs and some non-ARM microcontrollers).

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

Licensed under either of:

at your option.

[§](https://docs.rs#contribution)Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Simple usage (allocating, no associated data):

```
use aes_gcm::{
    aead::{Aead, AeadCore, KeyInit, OsRng},
    Aes256Gcm, Nonce, Key // Or `Aes128Gcm`
};
// The encryption key can be generated randomly:
let key = Aes256Gcm::generate_key(OsRng);
// Transformed from a byte array:
let key: &[u8; 32] = &[42; 32];
let key: &Key<Aes256Gcm> = key.into();
// Note that you can get byte array from slice using the `TryInto` trait:
let key: &[u8] = &[42; 32];
let key: [u8; 32] = key.try_into()?;
// Alternatively, the key can be transformed directly from a byte slice
// (panicks on length mismatch):
let key = Key::<Aes256Gcm>::from_slice(key);
let cipher = Aes256Gcm::new(&key);
let nonce = Aes256Gcm::generate_nonce(&mut OsRng); // 96-bits; unique per message
let ciphertext = cipher.encrypt(&nonce, b"plaintext message".as_ref())?;
let plaintext = cipher.decrypt(&nonce, ciphertext.as_ref())?;
assert_eq!(&plaintext, b"plaintext message");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-place-usage-eliminates-alloc-requirement)In-place Usage (eliminates `alloc` requirement)

This crate has an optional `alloc` feature which can be disabled in e.g.
microcontroller environments that don’t have a heap.

The [ AeadInPlace::encrypt_in_place](https://docs.rs/trait.AeadInPlace.html#method.encrypt_in_place) and

[methods accept any type that impls the](https://docs.rs/trait.AeadInPlace.html#method.decrypt_in_place)

`AeadInPlace::decrypt_in_place`[trait which contains the plaintext for encryption or ciphertext for decryption.](https://docs.rs/aead/0.5.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aead/trait.Buffer.html)

`aead::Buffer`Note that if you enable the `heapless` feature of this crate,
you will receive an impl of [ aead::Buffer](https://docs.rs/aead/0.5.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aead/trait.Buffer.html) for

`heapless::Vec`
(re-exported from the [crate as](https://docs.rs/aead/0.5.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aead/index.html)

`aead`[), which can then be passed as the](https://docs.rs/heapless/0.7.17/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/heapless/vec/struct.Vec.html)

`aead::heapless::Vec``buffer` parameter to the in-place encrypt
and decrypt methods:```
use aes_gcm::{
    aead::{AeadCore, AeadInPlace, KeyInit, OsRng, heapless::Vec},
    Aes256Gcm, Nonce, // Or `Aes128Gcm`
};
let key = Aes256Gcm::generate_key(&mut OsRng);
let cipher = Aes256Gcm::new(&key);
let nonce = Aes256Gcm::generate_nonce(&mut OsRng); // 96-bits; unique per message
let mut buffer: Vec<u8, 128> = Vec::new(); // Note: buffer needs 16-bytes overhead for auth tag
buffer.extend_from_slice(b"plaintext message");
// Encrypt `buffer` in-place, replacing the plaintext contents with ciphertext
cipher.encrypt_in_place(&nonce, b"", &mut buffer)?;
// `buffer` now contains the message ciphertext
assert_ne!(&buffer, b"plaintext message");
// Decrypt `buffer` in-place, replacing its ciphertext context with the original plaintext
cipher.decrypt_in_place(&nonce, b"", &mut buffer)?;
assert_eq!(&buffer, b"plaintext message");
```
Similarly, enabling the `arrayvec` feature of this crate will provide an impl of
[ aead::Buffer](https://docs.rs/aead/0.5.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aead/trait.Buffer.html) for

`arrayvec::ArrayVec` (re-exported from the [crate as](https://docs.rs/aead/0.5.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aead/index.html)

`aead`[).](https://docs.rs/arrayvec/0.7.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrayvec/arrayvec/struct.ArrayVec.html)

`aead::arrayvec::ArrayVec`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# anyhow - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/anyhow/^1.0/

## Expand description

This library provides [ anyhow::Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html), a trait object based error
type for easy idiomatic error handling in Rust applications.

[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Use `Result<T, anyhow::Error>`, or equivalently`anyhow::Result<T>`, as the return type of any fallible function.Within the function, use `?`to easily propagate any error that implements the`std::error::Error``use anyhow::Result; fn get_cluster_info() -> Result<ClusterMap> { let config = std::fs::read_to_string("cluster.json")?; let map: ClusterMap = serde_json::from_str(&config)?; Ok(map) }`
-
Attach context to help the person troubleshooting the error understand where things went wrong. A low-level error like “No such file or directory” can be annoying to debug without more context about what higher level step the application was in the middle of. `use anyhow::{Context, Result}; fn main() -> Result<()> { ... it.detach().context("Failed to detach the important thing")?; let content = std::fs::read(path) .with_context(|| format!("Failed to read instrs from {}", path))?; ... }``Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)`
-
Downcasting is supported and can be by value, by shared reference, or by mutable reference as needed. `// If the error was caused by redaction, then return a // tombstone instead of the content. match root_cause.downcast_ref::<DataStoreError>() { Some(DataStoreError::Censored(_)) => Ok(Poll::Ready(REDACTED_CONTENT)), None => Err(error), }`
-
If using Rust ≥ 1.65, a backtrace is captured and printed with the error if the underlying error type does not already provide its own. In order to see backtraces, they must be enabled through the environment variables described in `std::backtrace`- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only errors to have backtraces, set `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only panics to have backtraces, set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`and`RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`.

- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
-
Anyhow works with any error type that has an impl of `std::error::Error`, including ones defined in your crate. We do not bundle a`derive(Error)`macro but you can write the impls yourself or use a standalone macro like[thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror).`use thiserror::Error; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum FormatError { #[error("Invalid header (expected {expected:?}, got {found:?})")] InvalidHeader { expected: String, found: String, }, #[error("Missing attribute: {0}")] MissingAttribute(String), }`
-
One-off error messages can be constructed using the `anyhow!`macro, which supports string interpolation and produces an`anyhow::Error`.`return Err(anyhow!("Missing attribute: {}", missing));`A `bail!`macro is provided as a shorthand for the same early return.`bail!("Missing attribute: {}", missing);`

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

In no_std mode, almost all of the same API is available and works the same way. To depend on Anyhow in no_std mode, disable our default enabled “std” feature in Cargo.toml. A global allocator is required.

```
[dependencies]
anyhow = { version = "1.0", default-features = false }
```
With versions of Rust older than 1.81, no_std mode may require an additional
`.map_err(Error::msg)` when working with a non-Anyhow error type inside a
function that returns Anyhow’s error type, as the trait that `?`-based error
conversions are defined by is only available in std in those old versions.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [anyhow](https://docs.rs/macro.anyhow.html)as format_err;

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [anyhow](https://docs.rs/macro.anyhow.html)
- Construct an ad-hoc error from a string or existing non-`anyhow`error value.
- [bail](https://docs.rs/macro.bail.html)
- Return early with an error.
- [ensure](https://docs.rs/macro.ensure.html)
- Return early with an error if a condition is not satisfied.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Iterator of a chain of source errors.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- The `Error`type, a wrapper around a dynamic error type.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- Provides the `context`method for`Result`.

# argon2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/argon2/^0.5/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rustcrypto-argon2)RustCrypto: Argon2

Pure Rust implementation of the [Argon2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argon2) password hashing function.

[§](https://docs.rs#about)About

Argon2 is a memory-hard [key derivation function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_derivation_function) chosen as the winner of
the [Password Hashing Competition](https://www.password-hashing.net/) in July 2015.

It implements the following three algorithmic variants:

- **Argon2d**: maximizes resistance to GPU cracking attacks
- **Argon2i**: optimized to resist side-channel attacks
- **Argon2id**: (default) hybrid version combining both Argon2i and Argon2d

Support is provided for embedded (i.e. `no_std`) environments, including
ones without `alloc` support.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

Rust **1.65** or higher.

Minimum supported Rust version can be changed in the future, but it will be done with a minor version bump.

[§](https://docs.rs#semver-policy)SemVer Policy

- All on-by-default features of this library are covered by SemVer
- MSRV is considered exempt from SemVer as noted above

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

Licensed under either of:

at your option.

[§](https://docs.rs#contribution)Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#password-hashing)Password Hashing

This API hashes a password to a “PHC string” suitable for the purposes of password-based authentication. Do not use this API to derive cryptographic keys: see the “key derivation” usage example below.

```
use argon2::{
    password_hash::{
        rand_core::OsRng,
        PasswordHash, PasswordHasher, PasswordVerifier, SaltString
    },
    Argon2
};
let password = b"hunter42"; // Bad password; don't actually use!
let salt = SaltString::generate(&mut OsRng);
// Argon2 with default params (Argon2id v19)
let argon2 = Argon2::default();
// Hash password to PHC string ($argon2id$v=19$...)
let password_hash = argon2.hash_password(password, &salt)?.to_string();
// Verify password against PHC string.
//
// NOTE: hash params from `parsed_hash` are used instead of what is configured in the
// `Argon2` instance.
let parsed_hash = PasswordHash::new(&password_hash)?;
assert!(Argon2::default().verify_password(password, &parsed_hash).is_ok());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#key-derivation)Key Derivation

This API is useful for transforming a password into cryptographic keys for e.g. password-based encryption.

```
use argon2::Argon2;
let password = b"hunter42"; // Bad password; don't actually use!
let salt = b"example salt"; // Salt should be unique per password
let mut output_key_material = [0u8; 32]; // Can be any desired size
Argon2::default().hash_password_into(password, salt, &mut output_key_material)?;
```

- `pub use`- [password_hash](https://docs.rs/password-hash/0.5.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/password_hash/index.html);- `password-hash`

# ed25519_dalek - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ed25519-dalek/^2.0/

## Expand description

A Rust implementation of ed25519 key generation, signing, and verification.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Creating an ed25519 signature on a message is simple.

First, we need to generate a `SigningKey`, which includes both public and
secret halves of an asymmetric key.  To do so, we need a cryptographically
secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG). For this example, we’ll use
the operating system’s builtin PRNG:

```
// $ cargo add ed25519_dalek --features rand_core
use rand::rngs::OsRng;
use ed25519_dalek::SigningKey;
use ed25519_dalek::Signature;
let mut csprng = OsRng;
let signing_key: SigningKey = SigningKey::generate(&mut csprng);
```
We can now use this `signing_key` to sign a message:

```
use ed25519_dalek::{Signature, Signer};
let message: &[u8] = b"This is a test of the tsunami alert system.";
let signature: Signature = signing_key.sign(message);
```
As well as to verify that this is, indeed, a valid signature on
that `message`:

```
use ed25519_dalek::Verifier;
assert!(signing_key.verify(message, &signature).is_ok());
```
Anyone else, given the `public` half of the `signing_key` can also easily
verify this signature:

```
use ed25519_dalek::{VerifyingKey, Verifier};
let verifying_key: VerifyingKey = signing_key.verifying_key();
assert!(verifying_key.verify(message, &signature).is_ok());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#serialisation)Serialisation

`VerifyingKey`s, `SecretKey`s, `SigningKey`s, and `Signature`s can be serialised
into byte-arrays by calling `.to_bytes()`.  It’s perfectly acceptable and
safe to transfer and/or store those bytes.  (Of course, never transfer your
secret key to anyone else, since they will only need the public key to
verify your signatures!)

```
use ed25519_dalek::{PUBLIC_KEY_LENGTH, SECRET_KEY_LENGTH, KEYPAIR_LENGTH, SIGNATURE_LENGTH};
let verifying_key_bytes: [u8; PUBLIC_KEY_LENGTH] = signing_key.verifying_key().to_bytes();
let secret_key_bytes: [u8; SECRET_KEY_LENGTH] = signing_key.to_bytes();
let signing_key_bytes:    [u8; KEYPAIR_LENGTH]    = signing_key.to_keypair_bytes();
let signature_bytes:  [u8; SIGNATURE_LENGTH]  = signature.to_bytes();
```
And similarly, decoded from bytes with `::from_bytes()`:

```
let verifying_key: VerifyingKey = VerifyingKey::from_bytes(&verifying_key_bytes)?;
let signing_key: SigningKey = SigningKey::from_bytes(&signing_key_bytes);
let signature: Signature = Signature::try_from(&signature_bytes[..])?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pkcs8-key-encoding)PKCS#8 Key Encoding

PKCS#8 is a private key format with support for multiple algorithms. It can be encoded as binary (DER) or text (PEM).

You can recognize PEM-encoded PKCS#8 keys by the following:

`-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----`To use PKCS#8, you need to enable the `pkcs8` crate feature.

The following traits can be used to decode/encode [ SigningKey](https://docs.rs/struct.SigningKey.html) and

[as PKCS#8. Note that](https://docs.rs/struct.VerifyingKey.html)

`VerifyingKey`[is re-exported from the toplevel of the crate:](https://docs.rs/pkcs8/index.html)

`pkcs8`- `pkcs8::DecodePrivateKey`
- `pkcs8::EncodePrivateKey`
- `pkcs8::DecodePublicKey`
- `pkcs8::EncodePublicKey`

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

NOTE: this requires the `pem` crate feature.

```
use ed25519_dalek::{VerifyingKey, pkcs8::DecodePublicKey};
let pem = "-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
MCowBQYDK2VwAyEAGb9ECWmEzf6FQbrBZ9w7lshQhqowtrbLDFw4rXAxZuE=
-----END PUBLIC KEY-----";
let verifying_key = VerifyingKey::from_public_key_pem(pem)
    .expect("invalid public key PEM");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-serde)Using Serde

If you prefer the bytes to be wrapped in another serialisation format, all
types additionally come with built-in [serde](https://serde.rs) support by
building `ed25519-dalek` via:

`$ cargo build --features="serde"`They can be then serialised into any of the wire formats which serde supports.
For example, using [bincode](https://github.com/TyOverby/bincode):

```
use bincode::serialize;
let encoded_verifying_key: Vec<u8> = serialize(&verifying_key).unwrap();
let encoded_signature: Vec<u8> = serialize(&signature).unwrap();
```
After sending the `encoded_verifying_key` and `encoded_signature`, the
recipient may deserialise them and verify:

```
use bincode::deserialize;
let message: &[u8] = b"This is a test of the tsunami alert system.";
let decoded_verifying_key: VerifyingKey = deserialize(&encoded_verifying_key).unwrap();
let decoded_signature: Signature = deserialize(&encoded_signature).unwrap();
let verified: bool = decoded_verifying_key.verify(&message, &decoded_signature).is_ok();
assert!(verified);
```

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Digest](https://docs.rs/trait.Digest.html)
- Convenience wrapper trait covering functionality of cryptographic hash functions with fixed output size.
- [Digest](https://docs.rs/trait.DigestSigner.html)- Signer - `digest`
- Sign the given prehashed message `Digest``Self`.
- [Digest](https://docs.rs/trait.DigestVerifier.html)- Verifier - `digest`
- Verify the provided signature for the given prehashed message `Digest`
- [Signer](https://docs.rs/trait.Signer.html)
- Sign the provided message bytestring using `Self`(e.g. a cryptographic key or connection to an HSM), returning a digital signature.
- [Verifier](https://docs.rs/trait.Verifier.html)
- Verify the provided message bytestring using `Self`(e.g. a public key)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [verify_](https://docs.rs/fn.verify_batch.html)- batch - `batch`
- Verify a batch of `signatures`on`messages`with their respective`verifying_keys`.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Secret](https://docs.rs/type.SecretKey.html)- Key
- ed25519 secret key as defined in [RFC8032 § 5.1.5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032#section-5.1.5):
- [Sha512](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512.html)- `digest`
- SHA-512 hasher.
- [Signature](https://docs.rs/type.SignatureError.html)- Error
- Errors which may occur while processing signatures and keypairs.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

seeded by the system. Intended to be used in method chaining style,
e.g. `thread_rng().gen::<i32>()`, or cached locally, e.g.`let mut rng = thread_rng();`. Invoked by the`Default`trait, making`ThreadRng::default()`equivalent.

# tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/^3.8/

## Expand description

This is a library for creating temporary files and directories that are automatically deleted when no longer referenced (i.e., on drop).

- Use `tempfile()``std::fs::File`
- Use `NamedTempFile::new()`*named*temporary file that can be referred to its path.
- Use `tempdir()`
- Use `spooled_tempfile()`

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

This crate provides several approaches to creating temporary files and directories.
[ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) relies on the OS to remove the temporary file once the last handle is closed.

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`[both rely on Rust destructors for cleanup.](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

`tempfile` will (almost) never fail to cleanup temporary resources. However `TempDir` and
`NamedTempFile` will fail if their destructors don’t run. This is because `tempfile` relies on
the OS to cleanup the underlying file, while `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on rust
destructors to do so. Destructors may fail to run if the process exits through an unhandled
signal interrupt (like `SIGINT`), or if the instance is declared statically (like with
[ lazy_static](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/issues/62)), among other possible reasons.

[§](https://docs.rs#unexpected-file-deletion)Unexpected File Deletion

Most operating systems periodically clean up temporary files that haven’t been accessed recently
(often on the order of multiple days). This issue does not affect unnamed temporary files but
can invalidate the paths associated with named temporary files on Unix-like systems because the
temporary file can be unlinked from the filesystem while still open and in-use. See the
[temporary file cleaner](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners) section for more security implications.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This section discusses security issues relevant to Unix-like operating systems that use shared temporary directories by default. Importantly, it’s not relevant for Windows or macOS as both operating systems use private per-user temporary directories by default.

Applications can mitigate the issues described below by using [ env::override_temp_dir](https://docs.rs/env/fn.override_temp_dir.html) to
change the default temporary directory but should do so if and only if default the temporary
directory (

[) is unsuitable (is world readable, world writable, managed by a temporary file cleaner, etc.).](https://docs.rs/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`env::temp_dir`[§](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners)Temporary File Cleaners

In the presence of pathological temporary file cleaner, relying on file paths is unsafe because a temporary file cleaner could delete the temporary file which an attacker could then replace.

This isn’t an issue for [ tempfile](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) as it doesn’t rely on file paths. However,

[and temporary directories](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`*do*rely on file paths for

*some*operations. See the security documentation on the

[and the](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[types for more information.](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`Mitigation:

- This is rarely an issue for short-lived files as temporary file cleaners usually only remove temporary files that haven’t been modified or accessed within many (10-30) days.
- Very long lived temporary files should be placed in directories not managed by temporary file cleaners.

[§](https://docs.rs#access-permissions)Access Permissions

Temporary *files* created with this library are private by default on all operating systems.
However, temporary *directories* are created with the default permissions and will therefore be
world-readable by default unless the user has changed their umask and/or default temporary
directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#denial-of-service)Denial of Service

If the file-name randomness ([ Builder::rand_bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.rand_bytes)) is too small and/or this crate is built
without the

`getrandom` feature, it may be possible for an attacker to predict the random file
names chosen by this library, preventing temporary file creation by creating temporary files
with these predicted file names. By default, this library mitigates this denial of service
attack by:- Defaulting to 6 random characters per temporary file forcing an attacker to create billions of files before random collisions are expected (at which point you probably have larger problems).
- Re-seeding the random filename generator from system randomness after 3 failed attempts to
create temporary a file (when the `getrandom`feature is enabled as it is by default on all major platforms).

[§](https://docs.rs#early-drop-pitfall)Early drop pitfall

Because `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on their destructors for cleanup, this can lead
to an unexpected early removal of the directory/file, usually when working with APIs which are
generic over `AsRef<Path>`. Consider the following example:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::process::Command;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let temp_dir = tempdir()?;
// Spawn the `touch` command inside the temporary directory and collect the exit status
// Note that `temp_dir` is **not** moved into `current_dir`, but passed as a reference
let exit_status = Command::new("touch").arg("tmp").current_dir(&temp_dir).status()?;
assert!(exit_status.success());
```
This works because a reference to `temp_dir` is passed to `current_dir`, resulting in the
destructor of `temp_dir` being run after the `Command` has finished execution. Moving the
`TempDir` into the `current_dir` call would result in the `TempDir` being converted into
an internal representation, with the original value being dropped and the directory thus
being deleted, before the command can be executed.

The `touch` command would fail with an `No such file or directory` error.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a temporary file and write some data into it:

```
use tempfile::tempfile;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file = tempfile()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```
Create a named temporary file and open an independent file handle:

```
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
use std::io::{Write, Read};
let text = "Brian was here. Briefly.";
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file1 = NamedTempFile::new()?;
// Re-open it.
let mut file2 = file1.reopen()?;
// Write some test data to the first handle.
file1.write_all(text.as_bytes())?;
// Read the test data using the second handle.
let mut buf = String::new();
file2.read_to_string(&mut buf)?;
assert_eq!(buf, text);
```
Create a temporary directory and add a file to it:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let dir = tempdir()?;
let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// By closing the `TempDir` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the directory will still be deleted when `dir` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
// succeeded.
drop(file);
dir.close()?;
```

}## Expand description

Ed25519 keypair for signing and verifying Shard commits.
Generated on `shard init` and persisted to `.shard/keys/`.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.verifying_key)

`verifying_key: `[VerifyingKey](https://docs.rs/ed25519-dalek/2.2.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/ed25519_dalek/verifying/struct.VerifyingKey.html)Ed25519 verifying key — public, embedded in commits for cross-peer verification.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Save the keypair to `path/secret.key` (unencrypted) and `path/public.key`.

Save the keypair with passphrase-based encryption. When passphrase is empty, stores unencrypted (backward compatible).

# ordeal-lrat 0.3.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ordeal-lrat/0.3.0

Ordeal's LRAT certificate checker — **the sole trusted component**.

The ordeal solver is untrusted: an `Unsat` answer is believed only when
this checker has validated an LRAT certificate for it. This crate is
written to be translated to Lean 4 (via Aeneas) and formally verified, so
everything here is deliberately small, simple, and obviously correct:
no `unsafe`, no dependencies, no cleverness.

# Supported dialect: textual LRAT, **RUP-only**

**LOUD LIMITATION:** this checker supports only RUP (Reverse Unit
Propagation) addition steps. RAT steps — recognised by *negative* clause
ids in the hint list — are **rejected** with
[`CheckError::RatUnsupported`]. This is deliberate: ordeal's CDCL engine
emits RUP-only proofs, and rejecting is always sound (we may refuse a
valid certificate, we never accept an invalid one).

Accepted line forms (whitespace-separated integers, one step per line;
blank lines and lines starting with `c` are skipped as comments):

- Addition: `<id> <lit>* 0 <hint>* 0`— adds the clause`<lit>*`with id`<id>`, justified by unit propagation through the clauses named by`<hint>*`, in order.
- Deletion: `<id> d <id>* 0`— marks the named clauses dead. The leading`<id>`is informational (as emitted by drat-trim) and is not checked.

Clause ids are 1-based: original clause `i` of the input CNF (0-based)
has id `i + 1`; each addition step must then use exactly the next
sequential id (this is what ordeal emits; sparse ids are rejected).

# What "checked" means

An addition step `C` with hints `h1..hk` is verified by assuming the
negation of every literal of `C` and then unit-propagating through the
hint clauses in order: each hint must be either *falsified* (conflict —
the step is verified, so CNF ∧ ¬C is unsat, i.e. CNF ⊨ C) or *unit*
(its single unassigned literal is assigned true). Anything else —
a satisfied hint, a hint with two or more unassigned literals, running
out of hints, a dead or unknown id — rejects the certificate.

The whole certificate is accepted iff it parses in full AND some verified
addition step adds the **empty clause** (checking stops at that step;
parsed trailing steps are ignored). Parsing everything first is stricter
than strictly necessary and always sound (extra rejections only).

# Structure: parser vs kernel

The crate is split for the formal proof (issue #12): the [`kernel`]
module is the string-free checking core — the Aeneas → Lean translation
target carrying the soundness theorem — and this file is the untrusted
text parser feeding it. The CNF reaches the kernel directly, so parser
bugs cannot manufacture an acceptance (see `kernel` docs).

---

[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! bugs cannot manufacture an acceptance (see `kernel` docs).
[53](https://docs.rs#53)
[54](https://docs.rs#54)#![forbid(unsafe_code)]
[55](https://docs.rs#55)#![warn(missing_docs)]
[56](https://docs.rs#56)
[57](https://docs.rs#57)/// Why a certificate was rejected (or could not even be read).
[58](https://docs.rs#58)///
[59](https://docs.rs#59)/// Every variant carries the 1-based certificate line number where checking
[60](https://docs.rs#60)/// stopped, except [`CheckError::NoEmptyClause`] (a property of the whole
[61](https://docs.rs#61)/// certificate) and [`CheckError::InvalidCnfLiteral`] (a property of the
[62](https://docs.rs#62)/// input CNF).
[63](https://docs.rs#63)#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
[64](https://docs.rs#64)pub enum CheckError {
[65](https://docs.rs#65)    /// The input CNF itself is malformed: a clause contains the literal `0`
[66](https://docs.rs#66)    /// (or `i32::MIN`, whose negation would overflow).
[67](https://docs.rs#67)    InvalidCnfLiteral {
[68](https://docs.rs#68)        /// 0-based index of the offending clause in the input CNF.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)        clause_index: usize,
[70](https://docs.rs#70)    },
[71](https://docs.rs#71)    /// A certificate line could not be parsed.
[72](https://docs.rs#72)    Parse {
[73](https://docs.rs#73)        /// 1-based line number in the certificate text.
[74](https://docs.rs#74)        line: usize,
[75](https://docs.rs#75)        /// Human-readable description of the parse failure.
[76](https://docs.rs#76)        message: String,
[77](https://docs.rs#77)    },
[78](https://docs.rs#78)    /// An addition step did not use the next sequential clause id.
[79](https://docs.rs#79)    NonSequentialId {
[80](https://docs.rs#80)        /// 1-based line number in the certificate text.
[81](https://docs.rs#81)        line: usize,
[82](https://docs.rs#82)        /// The id this step was required to use.
[83](https://docs.rs#83)        expected: usize,
[84](https://docs.rs#84)        /// The id the step actually used.
[85](https://docs.rs#85)        found: usize,
[86](https://docs.rs#86)    },
[87](https://docs.rs#87)    /// A hint or deletion referenced an id that was never assigned.
[88](https://docs.rs#88)    UnknownId {
[89](https://docs.rs#89)        /// 1-based line number in the certificate text.
[90](https://docs.rs#90)        line: usize,
[91](https://docs.rs#91)        /// The unknown clause id.
[92](https://docs.rs#92)        id: usize,
[93](https://docs.rs#93)    },
[94](https://docs.rs#94)    /// A hint or deletion referenced a clause that was already deleted.
[95](https://docs.rs#95)    DeletedId {
[96](https://docs.rs#96)        /// 1-based line number in the certificate text.
[97](https://docs.rs#97)        line: usize,
[98](https://docs.rs#98)        /// The dead clause id.
[99](https://docs.rs#99)        id: usize,
[100](https://docs.rs#100)    },
[101](https://docs.rs#101)    /// A negative hint id was found: a RAT step, which this RUP-only
[102](https://docs.rs#102)    /// checker does not support (see the crate docs).
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    RatUnsupported {
[104](https://docs.rs#104)        /// 1-based line number in the certificate text.
[105](https://docs.rs#105)        line: usize,
[106](https://docs.rs#106)    },
[107](https://docs.rs#107)    /// A hint clause was neither unit nor falsified under the current
[108](https://docs.rs#108)    /// assignment (it was satisfied, or had two or more unassigned
[109](https://docs.rs#109)    /// literals), so unit propagation cannot use it.
[110](https://docs.rs#110)    HintNotUnit {
[111](https://docs.rs#111)        /// 1-based line number in the certificate text.
[112](https://docs.rs#112)        line: usize,
[113](https://docs.rs#113)        /// The id of the offending hint clause.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)        hint: usize,
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    },
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    /// The hint list ended before unit propagation reached a conflict, so
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    /// the addition step is not justified.
[118](https://docs.rs#118)    HintsExhausted {
[119](https://docs.rs#119)        /// 1-based line number in the certificate text.
[120](https://docs.rs#120)        line: usize,
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    },
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    /// The certificate ended without a verified addition of the empty
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    /// clause, so unsatisfiability was not established.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    NoEmptyClause,
[125](https://docs.rs#125)}
[126](https://docs.rs#126)
[127](https://docs.rs#127)impl core::fmt::Display for CheckError {
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> core::fmt::Result {
[129](https://docs.rs#129)        match self {
[130](https://docs.rs#130)            CheckError::InvalidCnfLiteral { clause_index } => {
[131](https://docs.rs#131)                write!(
[132](https://docs.rs#132)                    f,
[133](https://docs.rs#133)                    "input CNF clause {clause_index} contains an invalid literal"
[134](https://docs.rs#134)                )
[135](https://docs.rs#135)            }
[136](https://docs.rs#136)            CheckError::Parse { line, message } => {
[137](https://docs.rs#137)                write!(f, "line {line}: parse error: {message}")
[138](https://docs.rs#138)            }
[139](https://docs.rs#139)            CheckError::NonSequentialId {
[140](https://docs.rs#140)                line,
[141](https://docs.rs#141)                expected,
[142](https://docs.rs#142)                found,
[143](https://docs.rs#143)            } => {
[144](https://docs.rs#144)                write!(
[145](https://docs.rs#145)                    f,
[146](https://docs.rs#146)                    "line {line}: expected clause id {expected}, found {found}"
[147](https://docs.rs#147)                )
[148](https://docs.rs#148)            }
[149](https://docs.rs#149)            CheckError::UnknownId { line, id } => {
[150](https://docs.rs#150)                write!(f, "line {line}: unknown clause id {id}")
[151](https://docs.rs#151)            }
[152](https://docs.rs#152)            CheckError::DeletedId { line, id } => {
[153](https://docs.rs#153)                write!(f, "line {line}: clause id {id} was deleted")
[154](https://docs.rs#154)            }
[155](https://docs.rs#155)            CheckError::RatUnsupported { line } => {
[156](https://docs.rs#156)                write!(
[157](https://docs.rs#157)                    f,
[158](https://docs.rs#158)                    "line {line}: RAT step (negative hint) — this checker is RUP-only"
[159](https://docs.rs#159)                )
[160](https://docs.rs#160)            }
[161](https://docs.rs#161)            CheckError::HintNotUnit { line, hint } => {
[162](https://docs.rs#162)                write!(
[163](https://docs.rs#163)                    f,
[164](https://docs.rs#164)                    "line {line}: hint clause {hint} is neither unit nor falsified"
[165](https://docs.rs#165)                )
[166](https://docs.rs#166)            }
[167](https://docs.rs#167)            CheckError::HintsExhausted { line } => {
[168](https://docs.rs#168)                write!(
[169](https://docs.rs#169)                    f,
[170](https://docs.rs#170)                    "line {line}: hints exhausted without reaching a conflict"
[171](https://docs.rs#171)                )
[172](https://docs.rs#172)            }
[173](https://docs.rs#173)            CheckError::NoEmptyClause => {
[174](https://docs.rs#174)                write!(f, "certificate contains no verified empty-clause addition")
[175](https://docs.rs#175)            }
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        }
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    }
[178](https://docs.rs#178)}
[179](https://docs.rs#179)
[180](https://docs.rs#180)impl std::error::Error for CheckError {}
[181](https://docs.rs#181)
[182](https://docs.rs#182)pub mod kernel;
[183](https://docs.rs#183)
[184](https://docs.rs#184)use kernel::{CoreError, Step};
[185](https://docs.rs#185)
[186](https://docs.rs#186)/// Map a kernel rejection back onto certificate line numbers.
[187](https://docs.rs#187)///
[188](https://docs.rs#188)/// `lines[step]` is the 1-based certificate line the 0-based kernel step
[189](https://docs.rs#189)/// index came from.
[190](https://docs.rs#190)fn lift(err: CoreError, lines: &[usize]) -> CheckError {
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    let at = |step: usize| lines.get(step).copied().unwrap_or(0);
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    match err {
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        CoreError::InvalidCnfLiteral { clause_index } => {
[194](https://docs.rs#194)            CheckError::InvalidCnfLiteral { clause_index }
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        }
[196](https://docs.rs#196)        // Unreachable through `check` (parse_literal rejects 0 / i32::MIN
[197](https://docs.rs#197)        // before any Step is built), but the kernel validates independently
[198](https://docs.rs#198)        // and `lift` stays total.
[199](https://docs.rs#199)        CoreError::InvalidStepLiteral { step } => CheckError::Parse {
[200](https://docs.rs#200)            line: at(step),
[201](https://docs.rs#201)            message: "step clause contains an invalid literal".to_string(),
[202](https://docs.rs#202)        },
[203](https://docs.rs#203)        CoreError::NonSequentialId {
[204](https://docs.rs#204)            step,
[205](https://docs.rs#205)            expected,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)            found,
[207](https://docs.rs#207)        } => CheckError::NonSequentialId {
[208](https://docs.rs#208)            line: at(step),
[209](https://docs.rs#209)            expected,
[210](https://docs.rs#210)            found,
[211](https://docs.rs#211)        },
[212](https://docs.rs#212)        CoreError::UnknownId { step, id } => CheckError::UnknownId { line: at(step), id },
[213](https://docs.rs#213)        CoreError::DeletedId { step, id } => CheckError::DeletedId { line: at(step), id },
[214](https://docs.rs#214)        CoreError::HintNotUnit { step, hint } => CheckError::HintNotUnit {
[215](https://docs.rs#215)            line: at(step),
[216](https://docs.rs#216)            hint,
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        },
[218](https://docs.rs#218)        CoreError::HintsExhausted { step } => CheckError::HintsExhausted { line: at(step) },
[219](https://docs.rs#219)        CoreError::NoEmptyClause => CheckError::NoEmptyClause,
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    }
[221](https://docs.rs#221)}
[222](https://docs.rs#222)
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// Parse one whitespace token as a clause id (a positive integer).
[224](https://docs.rs#224)fn parse_id(token: &str, line: usize) -> Result<usize, CheckError> {
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    match token.parse::<usize>() {
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        Ok(id) if id >= 1 => Ok(id),
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        _ => Err(CheckError::Parse {
[228](https://docs.rs#228)            line,
[229](https://docs.rs#229)            message: format!("expected a positive clause id, found {token:?}"),
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        }),
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    }
[232](https://docs.rs#232)}
[233](https://docs.rs#233)
[234](https://docs.rs#234)/// Parse one whitespace token as a DIMACS literal (nonzero, negatable i32).
[235](https://docs.rs#235)fn parse_literal(token: &str, line: usize) -> Result<i32, CheckError> {
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    match token.parse::<i32>() {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        // `i32::MIN` is rejected because `-lit` must not overflow.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)        Ok(lit) if lit != 0 && lit != i32::MIN => Ok(lit),
[239](https://docs.rs#239)        _ => Err(CheckError::Parse {
[240](https://docs.rs#240)            line,
[241](https://docs.rs#241)            message: format!("expected a nonzero literal, found {token:?}"),
[242](https://docs.rs#242)        }),
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    }
[244](https://docs.rs#244)}
[245](https://docs.rs#245)
[246](https://docs.rs#246)/// Parse a deletion line body (the tokens after `<id> d`): a list of clause
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// ids terminated by `0`. Liveness of the ids is the kernel's concern.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)fn parse_deletion(tokens: &[&str], line: usize) -> Result<Vec<usize>, CheckError> {
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    let mut tokens = tokens.iter();
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    let mut ids: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    loop {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)        let Some(token) = tokens.next() else {
[253](https://docs.rs#253)            return Err(CheckError::Parse {
[254](https://docs.rs#254)                line,
[255](https://docs.rs#255)                message: "deletion line missing terminating 0".to_string(),
[256](https://docs.rs#256)            });
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        };
[258](https://docs.rs#258)        if *token == "0" {
[259](https://docs.rs#259)            break;
[260](https://docs.rs#260)        }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        ids.push(parse_id(token, line)?);
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    }
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    if tokens.next().is_some() {
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        return Err(CheckError::Parse {
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            line,
[266](https://docs.rs#266)            message: "trailing tokens after deletion terminator".to_string(),
[267](https://docs.rs#267)        });
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    }
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    Ok(ids)
[270](https://docs.rs#270)}
[271](https://docs.rs#271)
[272](https://docs.rs#272)/// Parse an addition line body (the tokens after `<id>`): the new clause's
[273](https://docs.rs#273)/// literals terminated by `0`, then the RUP hints terminated by `0`.
[274](https://docs.rs#274)/// Sequential-id and RUP checking are the kernel's concern; RAT detection
[275](https://docs.rs#275)/// (a negative hint id) happens here because sign lives in the text.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)fn parse_addition(tokens: &[&str], line: usize) -> Result<(Vec<i32>, Vec<usize>), CheckError> {
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    let mut tokens = tokens.iter();
[278](https://docs.rs#278)
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    // The new clause: literals up to the first `0`.
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    let mut new_clause: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    loop {
[282](https://docs.rs#282)        let Some(token) = tokens.next() else {
[283](https://docs.rs#283)            return Err(CheckError::Parse {
[284](https://docs.rs#284)                line,
[285](https://docs.rs#285)                message: "missing terminating 0 after clause literals".to_string(),
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            });
[287](https://docs.rs#287)        };
[288](https://docs.rs#288)        if *token == "0" {
[289](https://docs.rs#289)            break;
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        }
[291](https://docs.rs#291)        new_clause.push(parse_literal(token, line)?);
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    }
[293](https://docs.rs#293)
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    // The hints: clause ids up to the second `0`. A negative id marks a RAT
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    // step, which this RUP-only checker rejects (see the crate docs).
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    let mut hints: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    loop {
[298](https://docs.rs#298)        let Some(token) = tokens.next() else {
[299](https://docs.rs#299)            return Err(CheckError::Parse {
[300](https://docs.rs#300)                line,
[301](https://docs.rs#301)                message: "missing terminating 0 after hints".to_string(),
[302](https://docs.rs#302)            });
[303](https://docs.rs#303)        };
[304](https://docs.rs#304)        if *token == "0" {
[305](https://docs.rs#305)            break;
[306](https://docs.rs#306)        }
[307](https://docs.rs#307)        if token.starts_with('-') {
[308](https://docs.rs#308)            return Err(CheckError::RatUnsupported { line });
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        }
[310](https://docs.rs#310)        hints.push(parse_id(token, line)?);
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    }
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    if tokens.next().is_some() {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)        return Err(CheckError::Parse {
[314](https://docs.rs#314)            line,
[315](https://docs.rs#315)            message: "trailing tokens after hint terminator".to_string(),
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        });
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    }
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    Ok((new_clause, hints))
[319](https://docs.rs#319)}
[320](https://docs.rs#320)
[321](https://docs.rs#321)/// Parse a full certificate into kernel steps plus, per step, the 1-based
[322](https://docs.rs#322)/// certificate line it came from (for error reporting).
[323](https://docs.rs#323)fn parse_certificate(certificate: &str) -> Result<(Vec<Step>, Vec<usize>), CheckError> {
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    let mut steps: Vec<Step> = Vec::new();
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    let mut lines: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    for (line_index, raw_line) in certificate.lines().enumerate() {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)        let line = line_index + 1; // 1-based, for error reporting
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        let tokens: Vec<&str> = raw_line.split_whitespace().collect();
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        match tokens.first() {
[330](https://docs.rs#330)            None => continue,                                  // blank line
[331](https://docs.rs#331)            Some(first) if first.starts_with('c') => continue, // comment
[332](https://docs.rs#332)            Some(first) => {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)                let id = parse_id(first, line)?;
[334](https://docs.rs#334)                let step = if tokens.get(1) == Some(&"d") {
[335](https://docs.rs#335)                    // The leading id of a deletion line is informational.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)                    Step::Delete {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)                        ids: parse_deletion(&tokens[2..], line)?,
[338](https://docs.rs#338)                    }
[339](https://docs.rs#339)                } else {
[340](https://docs.rs#340)                    let (clause, hints) = parse_addition(&tokens[1..], line)?;
[341](https://docs.rs#341)                    Step::Add { id, clause, hints }
[342](https://docs.rs#342)                };
[343](https://docs.rs#343)                steps.push(step);
[344](https://docs.rs#344)                lines.push(line);
[345](https://docs.rs#345)            }
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        }
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    }
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    Ok((steps, lines))
[349](https://docs.rs#349)}
[350](https://docs.rs#350)
[351](https://docs.rs#351)/// Check a textual LRAT `certificate` against the input `cnf`.
[352](https://docs.rs#352)///
[353](https://docs.rs#353)/// `cnf` is the clause list in DIMACS literal convention (variable `v` is
[354](https://docs.rs#354)/// the literal `v`, its negation `-v`; `0` is not a literal). Clause ids in
[355](https://docs.rs#355)/// the certificate are 1-based: original clause `i` (0-based) has id
[356](https://docs.rs#356)/// `i + 1`, and added clauses take sequential ids after that.
[357](https://docs.rs#357)///
[358](https://docs.rs#358)/// Returns `Ok(())` iff the certificate contains a verified addition of the
[359](https://docs.rs#359)/// **empty clause**, which proves the CNF unsatisfiable. Any other outcome —
[360](https://docs.rs#360)/// including certificates that are merely *not understood* (parse errors,
[361](https://docs.rs#361)/// RAT steps) — is a rejection. Rejection never means "satisfiable"; it
[362](https://docs.rs#362)/// only means "not proven unsatisfiable by this certificate".
[363](https://docs.rs#363)pub fn check(cnf: &[Vec<i32>], certificate: &str) -> Result<(), CheckError> {
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    // Parse the whole certificate first (the untrusted, string-facing half),
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    // then run the string-free kernel (the Aeneas → Lean target) over the
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    // parsed steps. Soundness never depends on the parser: the CNF reaches
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    // the kernel directly, so a parser bug can only change WHICH steps get
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    // checked — every accepted certificate was still kernel-verified against
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    // the real CNF. See `kernel` module docs and issue #12.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    let (steps, lines) = parse_certificate(certificate)?;
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    kernel::check_steps(cnf, &steps).map_err(|e| lift(e, &lines))
[372](https://docs.rs#372)}
[373](https://docs.rs#373)
[374](https://docs.rs#374)#[cfg(test)]
[375](https://docs.rs#375)mod tests {
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    use super::*;
[377](https://docs.rs#377)
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    /// The 2-clause contradiction: (x1) ∧ (¬x1).
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    fn tiny_cnf() -> Vec<Vec<i32>> {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        vec![vec![1], vec![-1]]
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    }
[382](https://docs.rs#382)
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    /// The 4-clause full contradiction over x1, x2:
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    /// ids 1..=4 are [1,2], [-1,2], [1,-2], [-1,-2].
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    fn quad_cnf() -> Vec<Vec<i32>> {
[386](https://docs.rs#386)        vec![vec![1, 2], vec![-1, 2], vec![1, -2], vec![-1, -2]]
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    }
[388](https://docs.rs#388)
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    // ── Hand-verified ACCEPT cases (UV-011) ─────────────────────────────
[390](https://docs.rs#390)
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    /// (a) Empty clause directly from the two unit clauses: assuming
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    /// nothing, hint 1 = [1] is unit (assign x1), hint 2 = [-1] is
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    /// falsified — conflict, step verified.
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    #[test]
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    fn accepts_two_unit_contradiction() {
[396](https://docs.rs#396)        assert_eq!(check(&tiny_cnf(), "3 0 1 2 0"), Ok(()));
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    }
[398](https://docs.rs#398)
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// (b) Hand-derived RUP chain: first add [2] (assume ¬x2; hint 1 =
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    /// [1,2] is unit on x1; hint 2 = [-1,2] is falsified). Then the empty
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// clause (hint 5 = [2] is unit on x2; hint 3 = [1,-2] is unit on x1;
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    /// hint 4 = [-1,-2] is falsified).
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    #[test]
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    fn accepts_quad_cnf_rup_chain() {
[405](https://docs.rs#405)        let cert = "5 2 0 1 2 0\n6 0 5 3 4 0";
[406](https://docs.rs#406)        assert_eq!(check(&quad_cnf(), cert), Ok(()));
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    }
[408](https://docs.rs#408)
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    /// (c) Same proof with a deletion line in the middle: clauses 1 and 2
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// are dead by the final step, which only uses 5, 3, 4.
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    #[test]
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    fn accepts_proof_with_deletion() {
[413](https://docs.rs#413)        let cert = "5 2 0 1 2 0\n5 d 1 2 0\n6 0 5 3 4 0";
[414](https://docs.rs#414)        assert_eq!(check(&quad_cnf(), cert), Ok(()));
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    }
[416](https://docs.rs#416)
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    // ── Mutation REJECT cases (UV-011) ──────────────────────────────────
[418](https://docs.rs#418)
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    /// Dropped hint: without hint 4 the final chain propagates but never
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    /// reaches a conflict.
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    #[test]
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    fn rejects_dropped_hint() {
[423](https://docs.rs#423)        let cert = "5 2 0 1 2 0\n6 0 5 3 0";
[424](https://docs.rs#424)        assert_eq!(
[425](https://docs.rs#425)            check(&quad_cnf(), cert),
[426](https://docs.rs#426)            Err(CheckError::HintsExhausted { line: 2 })
[427](https://docs.rs#427)        );
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    }
[429](https://docs.rs#429)
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// Wrong hint order: hint 3 = [1,-2] comes first, but with nothing
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    /// assigned it has two unassigned literals — not unit, not falsified.
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    #[test]
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    fn rejects_wrong_hint_order() {
[434](https://docs.rs#434)        let cert = "5 2 0 1 2 0\n6 0 3 4 5 0";
[435](https://docs.rs#435)        assert_eq!(
[436](https://docs.rs#436)            check(&quad_cnf(), cert),
[437](https://docs.rs#437)            Err(CheckError::HintNotUnit { line: 2, hint: 3 })
[438](https://docs.rs#438)        );
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    }
[440](https://docs.rs#440)
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    /// Reference to a deleted clause: clause 3 is deleted, then used.
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    #[test]
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    fn rejects_deleted_clause_reference() {
[444](https://docs.rs#444)        let cert = "5 2 0 1 2 0\n5 d 3 0\n6 0 5 3 4 0";
[445](https://docs.rs#445)        assert_eq!(
[446](https://docs.rs#446)            check(&quad_cnf(), cert),
[447](https://docs.rs#447)            Err(CheckError::DeletedId { line: 3, id: 3 })
[448](https://docs.rs#448)        );
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    }
[450](https://docs.rs#450)
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    /// Reference to an id that was never assigned.
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    #[test]
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    fn rejects_unknown_id() {
[454](https://docs.rs#454)        assert_eq!(
[455](https://docs.rs#455)            check(&tiny_cnf(), "3 0 1 9 0"),
[456](https://docs.rs#456)            Err(CheckError::UnknownId { line: 1, id: 9 })
[457](https://docs.rs#457)        );
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    }
[459](https://docs.rs#459)
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    /// Truncated certificate: a valid step, but no empty clause ever.
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    #[test]
[462](https://docs.rs#462)    fn rejects_truncated_certificate() {
[463](https://docs.rs#463)        assert_eq!(
[464](https://docs.rs#464)            check(&quad_cnf(), "5 2 0 1 2 0"),
[465](https://docs.rs#465)            Err(CheckError::NoEmptyClause)
[466](https://docs.rs#466)        );
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    }
[468](https://docs.rs#468)
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    /// Certificate whose final (and only) added clause is non-empty: the
[470](https://docs.rs#470)    /// step itself verifies, but unsatisfiability is never established.
[471](https://docs.rs#471)    #[test]
[472](https://docs.rs#472)    fn rejects_final_clause_non_empty() {
[473](https://docs.rs#473)        // Adding [1]: assume ¬x1; hint 1 = [1] is falsified — verified.
[474](https://docs.rs#474)        assert_eq!(
[475](https://docs.rs#475)            check(&tiny_cnf(), "3 1 0 1 0"),
[476](https://docs.rs#476)            Err(CheckError::NoEmptyClause)
[477](https://docs.rs#477)        );
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    }
[479](https://docs.rs#479)
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    /// RAT-style negative hint: rejected as unsupported, never checked.
[481](https://docs.rs#481)    #[test]
[482](https://docs.rs#482)    fn rejects_rat_negative_hint() {
[483](https://docs.rs#483)        assert_eq!(
[484](https://docs.rs#484)            check(&tiny_cnf(), "3 0 1 -2 0"),
[485](https://docs.rs#485)            Err(CheckError::RatUnsupported { line: 1 })
[486](https://docs.rs#486)        );
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    }
[488](https://docs.rs#488)
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    /// Garbage text is a parse error, not a panic and not an accept.
[490](https://docs.rs#490)    #[test]
[491](https://docs.rs#491)    fn rejects_garbage_text() {
[492](https://docs.rs#492)        assert!(matches!(
[493](https://docs.rs#493)            check(&tiny_cnf(), "hello world"),
[494](https://docs.rs#494)            Err(CheckError::Parse { line: 1, .. })
[495](https://docs.rs#495)        ));
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    }
[497](https://docs.rs#497)
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    /// An addition step must use the next sequential id.
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    #[test]
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    fn rejects_non_sequential_id() {
[501](https://docs.rs#501)        assert_eq!(
[502](https://docs.rs#502)            check(&tiny_cnf(), "7 0 1 2 0"),
[503](https://docs.rs#503)            Err(CheckError::NonSequentialId {
[504](https://docs.rs#504)                line: 1,
[505](https://docs.rs#505)                expected: 3,
[506](https://docs.rs#506)                found: 7
[507](https://docs.rs#507)            })
[508](https://docs.rs#508)        );
[509](https://docs.rs#509)    }
[510](https://docs.rs#510)
[511](https://docs.rs#511)    // ── Dependency-graph guard (UV-011) ─────────────────────────────────
[512](https://docs.rs#512)
[513](https://docs.rs#513)    /// TRUST BOUNDARY GUARD: this crate must depend on nothing — in
[514](https://docs.rs#514)    /// particular not on the untrusted `ordeal` crate. The fact that this
[515](https://docs.rs#515)    /// test compiled at all already proves the crate builds without
[516](https://docs.rs#516)    /// `ordeal`; this assertion additionally pins the manifest to having
[517](https://docs.rs#517)    /// no `[dependencies]` table whatsoever.
[518](https://docs.rs#518)    #[test]
[519](https://docs.rs#519)    fn manifest_declares_no_dependencies() {
[520](https://docs.rs#520)        let manifest = include_str!("../Cargo.toml");
[521](https://docs.rs#521)        assert!(
[522](https://docs.rs#522)            !manifest.contains("[dependencies]"),
[523](https://docs.rs#523)            "ordeal-lrat must remain dependency-free: it is the trust boundary"
[524](https://docs.rs#524)        );
[525](https://docs.rs#525)        assert!(
[526](https://docs.rs#526)            !manifest.contains("ordeal\"") && !manifest.contains("ordeal ="),
[527](https://docs.rs#527)            "ordeal-lrat must not depend on the untrusted ordeal crate"
[528](https://docs.rs#528)        );
[529](https://docs.rs#529)    }

        clause_index:

[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),

}## Expand description

Why a certificate was rejected (or could not even be read).

Every variant carries the 1-based certificate line number where checking
stopped, except [ CheckError::NoEmptyClause](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckError.html#variant.NoEmptyClause) (a property of the whole
certificate) and

[(a property of the input CNF).](https://docs.rs/enum.CheckError.html#variant.InvalidCnfLiteral)

`CheckError::InvalidCnfLiteral`## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidCnfLiteral)

### InvalidCnfLiteral

The input CNF itself is malformed: a clause contains the literal `0`
(or `i32::MIN`, whose negation would overflow).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Parse)

### Parse

A certificate line could not be parsed.

#### Fields

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.NonSequentialId)

### NonSequentialId

An addition step did not use the next sequential clause id.

#### Fields

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.UnknownId)

### UnknownId

A hint or deletion referenced an id that was never assigned.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DeletedId)

### DeletedId

A hint or deletion referenced a clause that was already deleted.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.RatUnsupported)

### RatUnsupported

A negative hint id was found: a RAT step, which this RUP-only checker does not support (see the crate docs).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.HintNotUnit)

### HintNotUnit

A hint clause was neither unit nor falsified under the current assignment (it was satisfied, or had two or more unassigned literals), so unit propagation cannot use it.

#### Fields

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.HintsExhausted)

### HintsExhausted

The hint list ended before unit propagation reached a conflict, so the addition step is not justified.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.NoEmptyClause)

### NoEmptyClause

The certificate ended without a verified addition of the empty clause, so unsatisfiability was not established.

# ordeal_lrat::kernel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal-lrat/0.3.0/ordeal_lrat/kernel/index.html

## Expand description

The string-free checking core — **the Aeneas → Lean translation target**.

Everything semantic lives here, over already-parsed data: no `&str`, no
`String`, no formatting, no I/O. The soundness theorem (issue #12) is
stated about [ check_steps](https://docs.rs/fn.check_steps.html):

If

`check_steps(cnf, steps)`returns`Ok(())`, then`cnf`is unsatisfiable.

The text parser (in `lib.rs`) is **outside** this trusted core, and that
is sound by construction: the CNF reaches [ check_steps](https://docs.rs/fn.check_steps.html) directly (never
through the parser), so a buggy parser can only produce a

*different*step list — which still has to check against the real CNF — or reject. It can never manufacture an acceptance the core would not itself verify.

[§](https://docs.rs#style-constraints-aeneas)Style constraints (Aeneas)

This module is written in the fragment Aeneas translates cleanly today:
index-based `while` loops instead of iterators/closures, no early
`return` inside nested loops (every inner loop is its own function), no
slice patterns, and no std methods beyond `Vec::{new, push, len}` and
indexing. Keep it that way — a “cleanup” that reintroduces iterator
sugar breaks the translation.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Core](https://docs.rs/enum.CoreError.html)- Error
- Why the core rejected. Data-only (no strings) so the Lean model stays
simple; `step`is the 0-based index into the step list (the parser maps it back to a certificate line for reporting).
- [Step](https://docs.rs/enum.Step.html)
- One already-parsed certificate step.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_steps.html)- steps
- Check a parsed step list against the input CNF.

---

# check in ordeal_lrat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ordeal-lrat/0.3.0/ordeal_lrat/fn.check.html

## Expand description

Check a textual LRAT `certificate` against the input `cnf`.

`cnf` is the clause list in DIMACS literal convention (variable `v` is
the literal `v`, its negation `-v`; `0` is not a literal). Clause ids in
the certificate are 1-based: original clause `i` (0-based) has id
`i + 1`, and added clauses take sequential ids after that.

Returns `Ok(())` iff the certificate contains a verified addition of the
**empty clause**, which proves the CNF unsatisfiable. Any other outcome —
including certificates that are merely *not understood* (parse errors,
RAT steps) — is a rejection. Rejection never means “satisfiable”; it
only means “not proven unsatisfiable by this certificate”.

# cfg_if - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cfg-if/^1.0.4/

## Expand description

A macro for defining `#[cfg]` if-else statements.

The macro provided by this crate, `cfg_if`, is similar to the `if/elif` C
preprocessor macro by allowing definition of a cascade of `#[cfg]` cases,
emitting the implementation which matches first.

This allows you to conveniently provide a long list `#[cfg]`’d blocks of code
without having to rewrite each clause multiple times.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
cfg_if::cfg_if! {
    if #[cfg(unix)] {
        fn foo() { /* unix specific functionality */ }
    } else if #[cfg(target_pointer_width = "32")] {
        fn foo() { /* non-unix, 32-bit functionality */ }
    } else {
        fn foo() { /* fallback implementation */ }
    }
}
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [cfg_if](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_if.html)
- The main macro provided by this crate. See crate documentation for more information.

# proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1/

## Expand description

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler’s [ proc_macro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/index.html)
crate. This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
#[proc_macro_derive(MyDerive)]
pub fn my_derive(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    let input = proc_macro2::TokenStream::from(input);
    let output: proc_macro2::TokenStream = {
        /* transform input */
    };
    proc_macro::TokenStream::from(output)
}
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you’ll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to
propagate parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable
compiler API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not
exposed by proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly
compiler, the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to
rustc. We will polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As
these are unstable APIs that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of
proc-macro2 may make breaking changes to them at any time.

`RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build`Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-safety)Thread-Safety

Most types in this crate are `!Sync` because the underlying compiler
types make use of thread-local memory, meaning they cannot be accessed from
a different thread.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).
